meta.source: 99 Recipes Under 99 — Quick, Cheap and Ridiculously Easy Meals for Students Who Are Broke, Busy and Hungry

recipes.title: Bread Omelette Roll-Up
recipes.tagline: For the ten minutes between “I should eat” and “class starts.”
recipes.why_youll_love_it: This is an omelette and toast that decided to become one food instead of two separate things on a plate. You get the protein and richness of egg, the familiar comfort of bread, and a bit of crunch at the edges, all rolled into something you can genuinely eat with one hand while walking to class. It’s also forgiving: even if your first attempt looks a bit messy, it still tastes exactly right.
steps: Take a bowl. Crack one egg on the edge of the bowl — tap it firmly once, you’ll see a crack line appear — then use both thumbs to pull the shell open and let the egg fall into the bowl. Do the same with the second egg.
Pick up a fork. Beat the eggs for about 20 seconds, moving the fork in fast circles. Stop when the egg looks like one smooth, even yellow colour — no separate white streaks left.
Add the chopped onion, a small pinch of salt, and a small pinch of pepper into the same bowl. Stir it 4–5 times with the fork, just to mix it in. Set the bowl aside.
Now put your pan on the stove. Turn the flame to medium — not high, not low, right in the middle.
Pour 1 teaspoon of oil into the pan. Wait about 30 seconds. You’ll see the oil start to look thinner and move slightly when you tilt the pan — that means it’s hot enough now.

Pour the egg mixture into the pan all at once. As soon as it hits the pan, pick up the pan handle and tilt it gently in a circle for 2–3 seconds so the egg spreads out into one flat, even layer, like a thin sheet.
Put the pan back down. Do not touch it now. Let it sit undisturbed for 1 full minute.

After 1 minute, look at the top of the egg. It should still look a little wet and shiny in the middle — that’s normal, that’s what you want. Now take your 2 bread slices and lay them flat on top of the egg, side by side, gently pressing down with your fingers for a second so they stick to the egg.

Let this cook for 1 more minute without touching it. You’ll know it’s ready for the next step when you lift one corner of the egg gently with a spatula and see the underside has turned light golden — not brown, just golden.
Now slide your spatula all the way underneath the whole thing, egg and bread together. In one confident motion, flip it over, so the bread is now facing down into the pan and the egg is on top.
Let it cook for 30 more seconds. This just lightly toasts the bread side.
Turn off the stove. Use your spatula to slide the whole thing out onto a plate. While it’s still warm, roll it up from one end to the other, like a wrap. It’s ready to eat right now.
recipes.money_hack: Buy eggs by the tray (30) instead of loose — it works out noticeably cheaper per egg over a month.
recipes.swap_it: No onion? Skip it, or use a pinch of any dried herb you have.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Eggs — ₹14, Bread — ₹4, Onion — ₹1, Oil/salt — ₹1. Estimated total — ₹20.
recipes.closing_line: Eat it walking if you have to. Nobody’s judging.

recipes.title: Peanut Butter Banana Toast
recipes.tagline: Sweet, filling, and ready before your kettle even finishes boiling water for tea.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Bread, peanut butter, and banana is one of those combinations that just works — the peanut butter is thick and a little sticky, the banana is soft and cool, and the bread underneath holds it all together. This is the recipe for a morning when you genuinely have zero minutes to spare but still want something that feels like a real breakfast.

ingredients.raw: Pinch of salt (optional, makes the sweetness pop)
ingredients.name: salt

steps: If you have a toaster, put both bread slices in now and toast them. If you don’t have a toaster, this step is optional — you can skip straight to step 2 with plain bread and it still works fine.
Lay both bread slices flat on a plate.

Open your peanut butter jar. Using a butter knife or spoon, scoop out about ¾ tablespoon and spread it on the first slice — press and spread from the centre outward until it covers the whole slice, right to the corners. Do the same on the second slice.
Take the banana. Peel it by pinching the top and pulling the skin down in strips. Lay the peeled banana on a cutting board or plate.
Using a knife, cut the banana into round slices, about as thick as your little finger — roughly half a centimetre each. You should get around 10–12 slices from one banana.
Lay the banana slices evenly across one piece of the peanut-butter-covered bread, covering it edge to edge.
If using salt, take a tiny pinch between two fingers and sprinkle it lightly over the banana slices — just a light dusting, not a lot.
Place the second slice of bread on top, peanut-butter-side facing down, to close it into a sandwich. Press down very gently with your palm. Cut in half if you like, and eat.
recipes.money_hack: Buy the biggest peanut butter jar you can afford in one go — it’s always cheaper per spoon than a small jar, and it doesn’t spoil quickly.
recipes.swap_it: No banana? Try it with a drizzle of honey or jam instead.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Bread — ₹4, Peanut butter — ₹8, Banana — ₹6. Estimated total — ₹18.
recipes.closing_line: This one’s basically dessert pretending to be breakfast.

recipes.title: Curd Rice in a Bowl
recipes.tagline: The oldest comfort food trick in the book: leftover rice, curd, and five minutes.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Curd rice works precisely because it asks nothing of you — no heat, no real technique. It’s cooling rather than heavy, which makes it the specific thing your body wants after a spicy dinner, a long day, or an evening your stomach feels unsettled.

ingredients.raw: A few curry leaves or a pinch of mustard seeds
ingredients.name: few curry leaves

steps: Take your leftover rice and put it in a bowl. If it’s been in the fridge and feels cold and hard, that’s fine — we’ll fix that in the next step.

Using the back of a spoon, press down on the rice and mash it gently — not into a paste, just enough to break up the big clumps so you’re left with smaller, separate-ish grains. This takes about 15–20 presses.
Add the curd on top of the rice. Add a small pinch of salt.
Mix everything together with the spoon, stirring in circles, until the curd and rice are fully combined and you don’t see any dry white rice left uncoated. This takes about 30 seconds of stirring.
Look at the texture. If it feels too thick to easily eat with a spoon, add a small splash of water or milk — about 2 tablespoons — and stir again. Repeat if it’s still too thick.

This step is optional but recommended: heat a tiny pan on medium heat, add ½ teaspoon of oil, wait 20 seconds until it looks hot, then add a pinch of mustard seeds. Wait until you hear them start popping — like tiny crackling sounds, this takes about 10–15 seconds. Add the curry leaves right after (they will sizzle loudly, don’t worry, that’s normal), let them cook for 10 seconds, then turn off the heat and pour this entire mixture, oil and all, over your curd rice.
Sprinkle chopped coriander on top if you have it. Let the bowl sit for 2 minutes before eating — curd rice tastes better slightly less cold than straight from the fridge.
recipes.money_hack: Always cook a little extra rice at dinner — even half a cup extra means curd rice is ready in five minutes tomorrow.
recipes.swap_it: No curd? Plain yoghurt works exactly the same way.
recipes.closing_line: Cooling, simple, and exactly what a tired stomach wants.

recipes.title: Loaded Masala Maggi
recipes.tagline: The 2-minute noodles you already know, but with actual vegetables and actual flavour.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Everyone already knows how to make Maggi, which is exactly the problem — it’s so automatic that it rarely gets treated as a real meal. Adding an egg and whatever vegetables happen to be sitting in your fridge changes the entire eating experience.

ingredients.raw: A few pieces of any vegetable you have (capsicum, carrot, peas)
ingredients.name: few pieces of any vegetable you have

steps: Put a pan on the stove. Pour in 1.5 cups of water — if you don’t have a measuring cup, use a normal drinking glass, that’s roughly 1.5 glasses.
Turn the flame to high. Let the water heat up until you see big, rolling bubbles across the whole surface — this usually takes 3–4 minutes. That’s a proper boil, which is what you need.
Add the sliced onion and any hard vegetables (carrot, capsicum) into the boiling water. Let them cook for 1 minute — just stand near the stove, no need to do anything else.

Break the Maggi noodle block in half with your hands if you want shorter noodles (optional). Drop the noodles into the boiling water, then sprinkle in the full tastemaker packet, and add the chopped tomato too.
Set a timer for 2 minutes. Stir the noodles gently with a fork or spoon every 20–30 seconds so they don’t stick together in one clump at the bottom.
When the timer goes off, push all the noodles over to one side of the pan using your spoon, so there’s an empty space of broth on the other side.
Crack the egg directly into that empty space. Wait about 10 seconds without touching it — this lets the white firm up slightly.
Now break the yolk with your spoon and stir it around in that empty space for about 20 seconds, scrambling it into small pieces.
Mix the scrambled egg pieces through the rest of the noodles. Cook for 1 more minute, stirring occasionally.
Turn off the stove. Taste a tiny bit from the edge of the pan (careful, it’s hot) — if it tastes a little flat, add one more small pinch of salt. Pour into a bowl and eat.
recipes.money_hack: Buy Maggi in the 4-pack or family pack — it’s noticeably cheaper per packet than buying singles.
recipes.swap_it: No egg? Add a handful of crushed peanuts at the end for crunch and protein instead.
recipes.closing_line: Two-minute noodles, eight-minute satisfaction. Worth it.

recipes.title: Butter Masala Toast
recipes.tagline: For when you want “cheesy toast” flavours without buying actual cheese.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A generous amount of butter hitting a hot pan does most of the work that a more complicated recipe would need several ingredients to achieve. This is the toast you make when you want to feel like you tried, on a morning when you very much did not have time to try.

ingredients.raw: Pinch of chaat masala or red chilli powder
ingredients.name: chaat masala

steps: Take the butter straight from the fridge — don’t wait for it to soften, that’s not needed.

Using a butter knife, scoop about 1 teaspoon of butter and spread it over one whole side of the first bread slice. Press and spread it all the way to the corners and edges — don’t leave any bare spots, since bare spots dry out and taste plain. Repeat for the second slice.
Put a dry pan (no oil needed) on the stove. Turn the flame to medium.
Wait about 20 seconds, then hold your palm flat about 3 inches above the pan surface — if you feel warmth, the pan is ready. (Don’t touch the pan itself.)
Place both bread slices into the pan, butter-side facing down onto the hot pan.

While they cook, sprinkle a pinch of chaat masala and a pinch of salt evenly over the top (dry) side of each slice — this way the seasoning is already in place and you won’t need to reach for spice jars later while the pan is hot.

Let them cook undisturbed for about 2 minutes. After 2 minutes, use your spatula to lift one corner and peek underneath — you’re looking for an even golden-brown colour with maybe a few slightly darker spots. If it still looks pale, cook for another 30 seconds and check again.
Once golden, use the spatula to lift both slices out onto a plate. They’re ready to eat immediately.
recipes.money_hack: A small block of butter lasts weeks in this recipe — it’s cheaper per use than it looks on the shelf.
recipes.swap_it: No chaat masala? Plain chilli powder and salt does the job just as well.
recipes.closing_line: Small effort, disproportionately good result.

recipes.title: Quick Egg Bhurji Mash
recipes.tagline: Scrambled eggs’ more flavourful, more filling cousin.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Bhurji is what happens when scrambled eggs stop being an afterthought and start being the main event. This is genuinely one of the fastest ways to turn two eggs into something that feels like a proper cooked meal.
steps: Put your pan on the stove and turn the flame to medium. Add 1 teaspoon of oil.
Wait about 30 seconds for the oil to heat up — you’ll see it thin out and move easily when you tilt the pan slightly.
Add the chopped onion (and the chilli, if using) into the pan. Stir it with your spoon for the first few seconds so it doesn’t stick.

Let the onion cook for 2 minutes, stirring every 20–30 seconds. You want the onion to turn soft and slightly see-through at the edges — not brown, just soft. If it starts browning, turn your flame down a little.
Add the chopped tomato, a pinch of turmeric, a pinch of red chilli powder, and a pinch of salt. Stir everything together for a few seconds.
Let this cook for 1–2 minutes, stirring occasionally. You’re waiting for the tomato pieces to go soft and start breaking apart into a saucy texture, rather than staying firm.
Now crack both eggs directly into the pan, right on top of the onion-tomato mixture.
Wait about 5 seconds without touching anything — you’ll see the edges of the egg whites start turning from clear to white.

Using the edge of your spoon, start breaking the yolks and gently folding everything together — scoop from the bottom of the pan and fold it over the top, like you’re turning pages. Keep doing this slowly.

Keep folding and cooking for about 1 more minute. Stop when the eggs look mostly set but still slightly soft and a little glossy — not dry or rubbery. They’ll firm up a little more even after you take the pan off the heat.
Turn off the stove. Serve immediately, on its own or with bread.
recipes.money_hack: This is a great way to use up a tomato or onion that’s a day or two past its best.
recipes.swap_it: No tomato? It still works — just onion, chilli, and egg is a classic combination on its own.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Eggs — ₹14, Onion — ₹2, Tomato — ₹3, Spices/oil — ₹3. Estimated total — ₹22.
recipes.closing_line: Ten minutes of cooking for a meal that actually tastes looked-after.

recipes.title: Five-Minute Poha
recipes.tagline: Light, fast, and the closest thing to a “proper breakfast” you can make this quickly.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Poha barely needs cooking at all — the flattened rice is already par-cooked, so all you’re doing is rehydrating it and warming it through with a bit of spice. It’s genuinely light on the stomach.
steps: Put the poha into a sieve or colander (a strainer). Hold it under your tap and run cool water over it for about 10–15 seconds, moving the poha around gently with your other hand so the water reaches all of it.
Turn off the tap. Let the wet poha sit in the sieve for 1 minute — it will keep softening on its own during this time, so don’t worry if it still feels a bit firm right after rinsing.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium.

Wait 30 seconds for the oil to heat, then add a pinch of mustard seeds. Wait and listen — within 15–20 seconds you’ll hear them start popping and crackling, like tiny sparks. That’s your signal to move to the next step.
Add the chopped onion and chilli (if using). Stir and cook for about 2 minutes, until the onion turns soft.
Add a pinch of turmeric and a pinch of salt. Stir for 5 seconds — don’t let the spices sit alone on the hot pan too long or they can burn and taste bitter.
Add the softened poha from the sieve. Using your spoon, mix everything together gently — turn and fold rather than stir hard, since poha strands break easily if handled roughly.
Cook for 1 more minute, folding gently every 15 seconds, just to warm the poha through evenly.
Turn off the stove. If using lemon, cut it in half and squeeze one half over the poha now. Give it one final gentle toss, then serve.
recipes.money_hack: Poha is sold cheaply in bulk at most kirana stores — buying a 500g bag lasts many breakfasts.
recipes.swap_it: No mustard seeds? Skip the tempering step and just sauté the onion directly in oil.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Poha — ₹8, Onion — ₹2, Spices/oil — ₹3, Lemon — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹15.
recipes.closing_line: Light enough for a morning that already feels heavy.

recipes.title: Curd, Banana & Honey Bowl
recipes.tagline: No cooking, no cleanup, no excuses.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: There’s a specific kind of morning where even a five-minute recipe feels like too much, and this exists for exactly that morning — three ingredients, no heat, no pan to wash.
steps: Take a bowl. Spoon the curd into it first — about ¾ of a cup, or roughly 6 heaped spoonfuls.
Peel the banana by pinching the top and pulling the skin down. Place it on a cutting board.
Cut the banana into round slices, about half a centimetre thick, one by one, until the whole banana is sliced.
Lay the banana slices on top of the curd, arranging them so they cover most of the surface rather than piling in one spot.

Open your honey and, using a spoon, drizzle about 1 teaspoon over the top — move the spoon slowly back and forth as you pour so it spreads over the whole bowl instead of landing in one thick blob in the middle.
If using peanuts, take a small handful, place them between your fingers or in your palm, and crush them by pressing firmly — you’ll feel them break apart. Sprinkle the crushed pieces over the top.
Your bowl is ready — eat immediately with a spoon.
recipes.money_hack: Buy curd in the bigger 400g–500g tub instead of small cups — it’s meaningfully cheaper per spoon.
recipes.swap_it: No honey? A pinch of sugar or jaggery works fine.
recipes.closing_line: Three ingredients, zero stress. Sometimes that’s the whole win.

recipes.title: Bread Upma
recipes.tagline: Upma’s quicker, bread-based cousin — same comfort, less semolina-stirring.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: This version skips the traditional semolina and water-ratio fuss entirely by using torn bread, which already has structure and just needs a little moisture and spice. It’s also one of the best possible uses for bread that’s gone a bit stale.
steps: Take the 3 bread slices. Using your hands (not a knife), tear each slice into small, bite-sized pieces — roughly the size of a large postage stamp. Do this over a plate so all the pieces land together.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, turn the flame to medium, and wait 30 seconds for it to heat up.
Add a pinch of mustard seeds. Listen for the popping and crackling sound — this takes about 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and chilli. Stir and cook for 2 minutes, until the onion turns soft.
Add a pinch of turmeric and a pinch of salt. Stir for a few seconds.
Add the torn bread pieces into the pan.
Take a small splash of water — about 1 tablespoon, just a light sprinkle from your fingers or a spoon, not a pour — and drizzle it over the bread pieces.
Using your spoon, toss and fold everything together gently for about 2 minutes. You’re done when every piece of bread looks yellow-coated from the turmeric and feels warm all the way through.
Turn off the stove and serve immediately.
recipes.money_hack: This is the perfect use for bread that’s gone slightly stale — it works even better here than fresh bread.
recipes.swap_it: No mustard seeds? A pinch of cumin seeds works just as well in the tempering.
recipes.closing_line: Proof that ”stale bread” and ”no plan” can still become breakfast.

recipes.title: Tomato-Onion Chutney Sandwich
recipes.tagline: A cold sandwich that tastes like someone put actual thought into it.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A quick raw chutney made from finely chopped onion, tomato, and chilli gives you far more depth than plain ketchup, for almost no extra effort.
steps: On a cutting board, chop the onion as finely as you can — cut it into thin strips first, then turn it and chop across into small pieces. Put the chopped onion into a small bowl.
Do the same with the tomato — cut it into small pieces, roughly the same size as the onion pieces. Add it to the same bowl.
If using chilli, chop it very finely (small pieces, since it’s spicy) and add it too.
Add a pinch of salt and a pinch of chaat masala to the bowl. Mix everything together with a spoon for about 10 seconds.
Let this sit for 1–2 minutes if you have the time — this isn’t essential, but it helps the flavours combine a little.
Lay out 2 slices of bread on a plate. Using a spoon, spread the chutney mixture evenly across both slices, right to the edges.
Place the other 2 bread slices on top to close the sandwiches.

If you want it warm: put a pan on the stove with 1 teaspoon of oil, turn the flame to medium, wait 30 seconds for it to heat, then place the sandwiches in. Press down gently with your spatula. Cook for 1 minute, then flip and cook the other side for 1 minute too. If you’re happy eating it cold, skip this step entirely — just cut and eat.
recipes.money_hack: This chutney mix also works as a topping for Maggi, rice, or eggs — make a bit extra and reuse it.
recipes.swap_it: No chaat masala? A pinch of black pepper and a squeeze of lemon does something similar.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Bread — ₹8, Onion — ₹2, Tomato — ₹3, Spices — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹15.
recipes.closing_line: Cold, tangy, and ready before your roommate finishes complaining about their day.

recipes.title: Roasted Peanut Chaat
recipes.tagline: Crunchy, tangy, and dangerously easy to keep eating past the point of being hungry.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Crunchy plus tangy plus a little spicy is almost always more satisfying than any one of those alone. This is dangerously easy to keep nibbling well past the point where you meant to stop.
steps: Take a bowl. Add the roasted peanuts into it — about half a cup, or a small handful and a half.
On a cutting board, finely chop the onion and add it to the bowl.
Finely chop the tomato too, and add it in the same bowl.
Sprinkle a pinch of chaat masala and a pinch of salt over everything.
Cut a lemon in half. Squeeze one half firmly over the bowl, using your other hand cupped underneath to catch any seeds so they don’t fall in.
Using a spoon, toss everything together gently for about 10 seconds, until the masala and lemon juice are spread evenly through the mix.
If using coriander, sprinkle it on top now. Eat right away — don’t let it sit too long, since the peanuts start to soften once they touch the lemon juice.
recipes.money_hack: Buy roasted peanuts loose from a local vendor rather than packaged — usually cheaper for the same amount.
recipes.swap_it: No fresh tomato? Skip it — the peanuts, onion, and chaat masala still work well alone.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Peanuts — ₹6, Onion — ₹2, Tomato — ₹2, Masala/lemon — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹12.
recipes.closing_line: A snack that somehow also counts as a meal if you eat enough of it.

recipes.title: Jaggery Oats Bowl
recipes.tagline: Warm, sweet, and the closest thing to a hug you’ll get on a rainy evening.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Oats cooked slowly in milk thicken naturally into a comforting, porridge-like texture. Jaggery adds a deep, slightly caramel-like sweetness that pairs beautifully with the earthiness of oats.

ingredients.raw: 1 cup milk (or milk and water mixed)
ingredients.name: milk

steps: Pour 1 cup of milk into a small pan. Put it on the stove and turn the flame to medium.
Stay near the stove — don’t walk away. Watch the milk closely. After about 2 minutes, you’ll see small bubbles forming at the edges and steam rising — that means it’s warm and close to boiling.
The moment you see it starting to rise or bubble up, add the oats immediately and turn the flame down to low.
Stir the mixture for the first minute, about every 20–30 seconds, so the oats don’t settle and stick to the bottom of the pan.
Let it cook for another 2–3 minutes on low heat, stirring every 30 seconds. You’re watching for the mixture to thicken — it should coat the back of your spoon rather than drip straight off.
Add the jaggery (grate or crush it first if it’s in a hard block) and the cardamom, if using. Stir well.
Cook for 1 more minute, stirring, until you can’t see any gritty jaggery bits left — it should be fully melted into the mixture.
Turn off the stove. Taste a small spoonful (careful, it’s hot) — add a little more jaggery if you want it sweeter. Pour into a bowl and eat while warm.
recipes.money_hack: Jaggery keeps for months unrefrigerated — buying a small block is cheaper long-term than buying sugar sachets.
recipes.swap_it: No milk? Make it with water — less creamy, but still warm and comforting.
recipes.closing_line: This is what ”everything’s going to be fine” tastes like.

recipes.title: Boiled Chana Chaat
recipes.tagline: High-protein, filling, and mostly just requires you to open a can or boil some chickpeas in advance.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Once chickpeas are boiled, this recipe is really just assembly. The combination of tang, sharpness, and savoury-sour chaat masala wakes up what would otherwise be a fairly plain ingredient.
steps: If your boiled chickpeas are cold from the fridge, put them in a sieve and run warm tap water over them for about 20 seconds — this takes the chill off and makes them taste better.
Let them drain in the sieve for a minute, then tip them into a bowl.
Finely chop the onion on a cutting board and add it to the bowl.
Finely chop the tomato too, and add it in.
Sprinkle a pinch of chaat masala and a pinch of salt over the top.
Cut a lemon in half. Squeeze one half over the bowl — chickpeas can handle a good amount of lemon, so don’t be shy, use the whole half.
Toss everything together gently with a spoon for about 10 seconds, making sure the masala coats everything rather than sitting at the bottom.
Sprinkle coriander on top if using, and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Boil a big batch of chickpeas once a week (soak overnight, boil 20–25 minutes) and refrigerate — then this recipe becomes a 5-minute assembly job all week.
recipes.swap_it: No fresh chickpeas boiled? Canned chickpeas work just as well — rinse them first.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Chickpeas — ₹10, Onion — ₹2, Tomato — ₹2, Masala/lemon — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹16.
recipes.closing_line: Protein, crunch, and tang — this one actually keeps you full.

recipes.title: Garlic Butter Toast
recipes.tagline: Simple, fragrant, and makes your room smell like you have your life together.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Garlic and butter cooked together release an aroma that’s disproportionately impressive for how little effort it takes.
steps: Take one garlic clove. Peel off the papery skin with your fingers or the flat side of a knife. Place the peeled clove on a cutting board.
Using a knife, chop the garlic as finely as you can — cut it into thin slices first, then chop across into tiny pieces. Keep chopping until the pieces are very small.
Put 1 teaspoon of butter into a small bowl. Add the chopped garlic. Mix them together thoroughly with a spoon until the garlic is evenly spread through the butter, not sitting in one clump.
Using a knife, spread the garlic butter over one side of each bread slice, covering right to the edges.
Put a dry pan on the stove (no extra oil needed) and turn the flame to medium.
Place both bread slices into the pan, butter-side facing down. Let them sit undisturbed — don’t move them around.

Cook for about 2 minutes. Then lift one corner with your spatula to check underneath — you want an even golden colour, with the garlic bits looking just slightly browned, not black. If it’s not golden yet, cook another 30 seconds and check again.
Once golden, remove from the pan immediately. While still hot, sprinkle a pinch of salt and chilli flakes over the top — the heat helps the seasoning stick.
recipes.money_hack: A whole bulb of garlic costs very little and lasts weeks — worth keeping on hand just for recipes like this.
recipes.swap_it: No fresh garlic? A pinch of garlic powder mixed into the butter works almost as well.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Bread — ₹4, Butter — ₹6, Garlic — ₹2, Spices — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹14.
recipes.closing_line: Smells like effort. Took none.

recipes.title: Hot Masala Milk with Biscuits
recipes.tagline: Not really a meal, but on the nights you’re too tired to chew much else, this counts.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: There’s a specific kind of tiredness where even chewing feels like effort, and warm, mildly spiced milk with something to dunk in it is exactly the right register for that mood.
steps: Pour 1 cup of milk into a small pan. Place it on the stove and turn the flame to medium.

Stay right next to the stove for this whole step — don’t walk away, even for a minute. Milk can rise up and spill over the sides very quickly, within about 30 seconds of starting to boil, with no warning.
Watch for small bubbles forming around the edges of the pan and steam starting to rise — this usually takes about 2 minutes.
The moment you see it about to rise up, add a pinch of turmeric or cardamom (whichever you’re using) and the sugar if using. Stir once with a spoon.
Turn the flame down to low. Let it simmer gently — small bubbles, not a big rolling boil — for about 1 minute, so the spice flavour has time to mix into the milk.
Turn off the stove. Carefully pour the hot milk into a mug, leaving a little space at the top so it doesn’t spill.

Take one biscuit. Dip it into the milk and hold it there for 2–3 seconds — count “one, two, three” in your head — then take it out and eat it before it gets too soft and breaks apart. Repeat with each biscuit.
recipes.money_hack: A packet of basic biscuits is one of the cheapest snacks per piece in any Indian kirana store — always worth keeping a pack around.
recipes.swap_it: No cardamom or turmeric? Even plain warm milk with sugar does the comfort-food job.
recipes.closing_line: Some nights, warm milk and biscuits is the whole meal. That’s allowed.

recipes.title: Mashed Potato Stuffed Roti
recipes.tagline: A shortcut aloo paratha for people who don’t have the energy to actually stuff and roll dough.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: This version skips the stuffing step entirely by mixing the mashed potato straight into the dough, so you get the exact same flavour with none of the fiddly technique. It’s a slightly denser, more rustic flatbread, and it’s far more forgiving if your rolling isn’t perfectly even.
steps: Make sure your boiled potato has cooled down — if it’s still hot, wait 5 minutes before touching it, since a hot potato makes the dough sticky.

Put the potato in a bowl. Using a fork, mash it by pressing down firmly and moving it around, until there are no big lumps left — small soft lumps are fine, big chunks are not, since they’ll tear the dough later.
Add the atta into the same bowl, along with the chopped onion, chilli powder, and a pinch of salt.
Using your fingers, rub and mix everything together for about 30 seconds — it should look like uneven, crumbly bits, not smooth yet.

Add water, just 1 tablespoon at a time. After each spoon, knead the dough with both hands for 15–20 seconds — press it, fold it, press again. Keep adding water slowly like this until the dough turns into one smooth, soft ball that doesn’t stick to your palm when you touch it. This usually takes about 4–5 tablespoons of water total.
Divide the dough into 2 equal balls, roughly the size of a small lemon each.
Sprinkle a little dry flour onto your rolling surface. Place one dough ball on it and flatten it slightly with your palm.

Using a rolling pin, roll it out evenly in all directions — roll once, then turn the dough a quarter turn, then roll again. Keep repeating this turning-and-rolling until you have a round flatbread about the size of a small plate.

Put your tawa or pan on the stove and turn the flame to medium. Wait about 1 minute for it to heat up — you can test it by flicking a few drops of water onto it; if they sizzle and disappear quickly, it’s ready.
Place the rolled roti onto the hot tawa. Let it cook for about 30 seconds, then flip it over using a spatula.
Add ½ teaspoon of oil or ghee on top and spread it lightly with the back of your spoon. Let it cook for 1 minute, pressing gently around the edges with your spatula.

Flip again, add a little oil to this side too, and cook for another minute. You’re looking for light golden-brown spots appearing on the surface — once you see those on both sides, it’s done. Repeat steps 7–12 with the second dough ball.
recipes.money_hack: Boil two or three extra potatoes whenever you’re already boiling one — they keep for a couple of days and make this recipe a five-minute job next time.
recipes.swap_it: No potato on hand? Use mashed, cooked dal instead for a different but equally filling version.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Atta — ₹6, Potato — ₹4, Onion — ₹2, Spices/oil — ₹6. Estimated total — ₹18.
recipes.closing_line: Tastes like effort. Took about fifteen minutes.

recipes.title: Sooji Uttapam
recipes.tagline: A thick, savoury pancake made from semolina — crispy edges, soft middle.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: This sooji-based version gets you most of the way to a real South Indian uttapam in twelve minutes — the semolina swells and softens as it rests in curd, giving you a batter that fries up with crisp edges and a soft, slightly spongy centre, without any waiting for fermentation.
steps: Put the sooji into a mixing bowl. Add the curd and a pinch of salt.

Stir with a spoon, then start adding water — just a splash at a time, about 1 tablespoon each time — stirring after each addition. Keep going until you get a batter about as thick as pancake batter: it should drop off your spoon slowly in a ribbon, not pour like water and not sit like a paste.
Now leave the bowl alone for exactly 5 minutes. Set a timer if you need to — don’t skip this rest, it’s what softens the semolina properly.
After 5 minutes, check the batter. If it’s thickened up too much while sitting, stir in one more small splash of water.
Add the chopped onion and tomato into the batter and stir them through evenly.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.

Pour the batter into the centre of the pan. Using the back of your spoon or ladle, spread it outward in a gentle circular motion, making a thick circle about the size of a small plate — don’t spread it too thin, uttapam should stay fluffy in the middle.

Let it cook undisturbed for 3 minutes. Do not touch it during this time. You’ll know it’s ready to flip when you see the edges turning dry-looking and starting to lift slightly away from the pan on their own.
Slide a wide spatula fully underneath, and flip it over in one motion.
Cook the second side for 2 minutes, pressing down very lightly with your spatula here and there so it makes good contact with the pan.
Once both sides show golden-brown patches, slide it onto a plate and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Sooji is one of the cheapest grains per kilo in most kirana stores — a small bag lasts for many breakfasts.
recipes.swap_it: No curd? Use water instead, though curd gives a slightly softer texture.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Sooji — ₹6, Curd — ₹5, Vegetables — ₹3, Oil — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹16.
recipes.closing_line: Crispy edges, soft middle, ready before your tea gets cold.

recipes.title: Eggless Banana Pancakes
recipes.tagline: Sweet, soft, and doesn’t need eggs, a whisk, or any real pancake skills.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Mashed banana does two jobs at once here — it binds the batter together and adds enough natural sweetness that you barely need added sugar. The riper the banana, the better, so the ones with brown spots are actually perfect.

ingredients.raw: ½ cup atta or plain flour
ingredients.name: atta

ingredients.raw: ¼ cup milk (adjust for batter thickness)
ingredients.name: milk

ingredients.raw: Pinch of cinnamon or cardamom powder (optional)
ingredients.name: cinnamon

steps: Peel the banana and put it in a bowl. Using a fork, mash it by pressing down repeatedly until it’s mostly smooth, with just a few tiny soft lumps left — don’t worry about getting it perfectly smooth.
Add the flour, milk, and cinnamon (if using) into the same bowl.
Stir with a spoon just until you can’t see any dry flour anymore — about 10–15 stirs. Stop as soon as it looks combined; stirring more than needed makes the pancakes tougher.

Put your pan on the stove and add a little oil or ghee, spreading it around with a spoon. Turn the flame to low-medium — lower than you might expect, since these brown fast on the outside but need gentle heat to cook through.
Wait 30 seconds for the pan to warm up.

Using a spoon, scoop out a small amount of batter — about 2 tablespoons — and pour it into the pan, making a small circle no bigger than your palm. Repeat with the rest of the batter if your pan has room for more than one at a time.
Let it sit undisturbed. After about 1½ minutes, look at the surface — you’ll see small bubbles forming and staying open, like tiny craters. That’s your sign it’s ready to flip.
Slide a thin spatula underneath and flip it in one smooth motion.
Cook the second side for another 1–1½ minutes. It’s done when it springs back gently if you press the centre lightly with your finger.
Lift it out onto a plate. Repeat with any remaining batter.
recipes.money_hack: Overripe bananas — the ones with brown spots you’d normally skip — actually work best here since they’re sweeter and mash more easily.
recipes.swap_it: No milk? Water works, though the pancakes will be slightly less rich.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Banana — ₹6, Flour — ₹4, Milk — ₹4, Oil — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹16.
recipes.closing_line: Sweet enough to feel like a treat, simple enough to make with your eyes half-closed.

recipes.title: Loaded Masala Omelette with Toast
recipes.tagline: A proper sit-down breakfast, still done in under ten minutes.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: This is the breakfast for the rare morning you actually have ten spare minutes and want to use them properly — a well-spiced omelette next to warm, buttered toast, timed so both finish together.
steps: Crack both eggs into a bowl. Beat them with a fork for about 20 seconds until smooth and evenly yellow.
Add the onion, tomato, chilli (if using), turmeric, salt, and pepper. Stir it all together for about 10 seconds so the colour looks uniform.
Spread butter on one side of each bread slice now, before you start cooking anything — this saves you from doing it later with messy hands.
Put a pan on the stove with 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for the oil to heat.
Pour the egg mixture into the pan and tilt the pan gently to spread it evenly across the bottom.

While the egg cooks, put a second dry pan (or the same pan later, once the egg is out) on another burner if you have one, or set the bread aside to toast right after — place the buttered bread in, butter-side down, and let it toast for about 2 minutes until golden, then remove and set aside.
Back to the egg: let it cook undisturbed for about 2 minutes. You’ll know it’s close to ready when the edges look fully set and only the very centre still looks a little glossy.
Slide your spatula underneath, supporting the egg fully so it doesn’t fold on itself, and flip it over in one motion.
Cook the second side for 1 more minute.
Slide the omelette onto a plate next to the toast. Serve both together while still hot.
recipes.money_hack: Buttering bread before toasting (rather than after) uses less butter overall and toasts more evenly.
recipes.swap_it: No tomato? Just onion and chilli still makes a great masala omelette.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Eggs — ₹14, Vegetables — ₹4, Bread — ₹4, Butter/oil — ₹6. Estimated total — ₹28.
recipes.closing_line: This is the breakfast that makes you feel like an adult who has it together.

recipes.title: Besan Chilla
recipes.tagline: A savoury gram-flour pancake — naturally vegetarian, naturally high-protein, genuinely tasty.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Besan batter firms up almost immediately in a hot pan and crisps beautifully at the edges, which is what makes chilla such a satisfying egg-free alternative to an omelette.
steps: Put the besan in a bowl. Add water a little at a time — about 2 tablespoons at first — and stir with a spoon or whisk after each addition, pressing out any lumps against the side of the bowl.
Keep adding water slowly and stirring until you get a smooth batter with the thickness of heavy cream — it should pour off your spoon in a steady stream, with no lumps anywhere.
Add the onion, tomato, chilli, turmeric, chilli powder, and salt. Stir until evenly mixed through.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.

Pour a ladleful of batter into the centre of the pan. Immediately, using the back of the ladle, spread it outward in a circular motion from the centre, working your way out to the edges, making one thin, even layer.
Let it cook undisturbed. Watch for the edges to start looking dry and slightly curling upward, and small holes may appear on the surface — this usually takes about 2 minutes.
Slide a wide, flat spatula underneath in one motion and flip it confidently — don’t hesitate halfway, a quick, decisive flip works best.
Cook the second side for about 1½ minutes, until it’s golden with a few darker crisp spots.
Slide it onto a plate and serve hot.
recipes.money_hack: Besan is cheap, keeps for months in a sealed container, and works in dozens of recipes — always worth having a bag around.
recipes.swap_it: No fresh vegetables? A plain besan chilla with just spices is still tasty on its own.
recipes.closing_line: Vegetarian, protein-rich, and doesn’t taste like either of those things is the point.

recipes.title: Overnight Oats (Prep Tonight, Eat Tomorrow)
recipes.tagline: Zero-effort breakfast because all the effort happened the night before.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Oats left to soak overnight in milk or curd soften completely through a slow, cold process, so by morning they’re creamy and ready without ever touching a stove.

ingredients.raw: ¾ cup milk or curd (or a mix of both)
ingredients.name: milk

ingredients.raw: A few banana slices or any fruit you have
ingredients.name: few banana slices

steps: Find a container with a lid — a small box, a jar, or even a bowl you can cover with a plate.
Add the oats into the container.
Pour in the milk or curd.
Add the honey.
Using a spoon, stir everything together thoroughly for about 15–20 seconds, making sure to scrape the sides so no dry oats are left clinging there uncovered.
Put the lid on (or cover with a plate). Place it in the fridge.
Leave it there overnight — at least 6 hours if possible, though even 3–4 hours works if you’re prepping in the evening for a late morning.
In the morning, take it out. Don’t be alarmed if it looks thick — that’s exactly right, it means the oats have absorbed the liquid properly.
Stir it well with a spoon to loosen it up.
Slice your banana or other fruit now, right before eating, and place the slices on top. Sprinkle with cinnamon if using. Eat cold, straight from the container.
recipes.money_hack: No fridge? Skip the milk and use only curd — it holds up better overnight at room temperature in cooler weather. In hot weather, this recipe is safest with fridge access.
recipes.swap_it: No fruit? A spoon of jam or a few crushed peanuts on top works just as well.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Oats — ₹6, Milk/curd — ₹8, Honey — ₹2, Fruit — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹18.
recipes.closing_line: You already did the work. Past-you deserves a thank you.

recipes.title: Sprouted Moong Breakfast Bowl
recipes.tagline: Crunchy, light, and quietly one of the more filling things on this list.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Sprouted moong is crisp and light rather than firm and starchy, which is part of why this bowl feels so much lighter to eat than the same beans boiled whole.
steps: If your sprouts have been in the fridge, put them in a sieve and rinse them under cool running water for about 10 seconds. Shake the sieve gently to remove excess water.
Tip the rinsed sprouts into a bowl.
Finely chop the onion and add it in.
Finely chop the tomato and add it in too.
Sprinkle a pinch of chaat masala and a pinch of salt over the top.
Cut a lemon in half and squeeze one half over the bowl.
Toss everything together gently with a spoon — turn and fold rather than stir hard, so you don’t crush the sprouts.
Sprinkle coriander on top if using, and eat within the next few minutes while everything’s still fresh.
recipes.money_hack: To sprout moong at home: soak dried moong overnight, drain, and leave in a covered container for 1–2 days, rinsing once a day, until small sprouts appear. Costs far less than store-bought sprouts.
recipes.swap_it: No sprouts? Boiled chickpeas or boiled moong (unsprouted) work as a substitute with a similar texture.
recipes.closing_line: Crunchy, light, and it’ll actually keep you full till lunch.

recipes.title: Egg Bhurji Roti Wrap
recipes.tagline: Yesterday’s bhurji logic, wrapped into today’s breakfast-on-the-go.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A roti holds its shape far better than bread when rolled tightly around a filling, so this genuinely stays together while you eat it one-handed on your way out.
steps: Put a pan on the stove with 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Add the chopped onion. Stir and cook for about 1 minute — just until it softens slightly and turns a little see-through at the edges. Don’t let it brown.
Add the turmeric, chilli powder, and a pinch of salt. Stir for a few seconds.
Crack both eggs directly into the pan. Wait 5 seconds, then start breaking the yolks and folding everything together gently with your spoon.
Keep folding for about 1 minute, until the eggs are just set — soft, not dry. Turn off the stove.

Take the roti. Place it directly over a low flame for about 5 seconds on one side, using tongs to hold it, then flip and do the other side for 5 seconds too — this makes it soft and bendy. (If you don’t have an open flame, warm it in a dry pan for about 20 seconds on each side instead.)
Lay the warm roti flat on a plate. Spoon the bhurji onto it in a line, positioned slightly off-centre rather than in the middle.
Fold the shorter, nearer edge of the roti up and over the filling first.
Continue rolling it the rest of the way into a tight roll, tucking in as you go so nothing falls out.
recipes.money_hack: Leftover rotis from last night’s dinner are perfect here — this is a great way to avoid roti going to waste.
recipes.swap_it: No roti on hand? Use two slices of bread instead, folded over the bhurji like a sandwich.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Eggs — ₹14, Onion — ₹2, Spices/oil — ₹3, Roti — ₹5. Estimated total — ₹24.
recipes.closing_line: Breakfast you can eat with one hand while packing your bag with the other.

recipes.title: Vermicelli Upma (Semiya)
recipes.tagline: Thinner, lighter, and cooks even faster than regular upma.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Vermicelli cooks almost as fast as instant noodles but tastes like a proper South Indian breakfast — light, mildly spiced, and easy on a sleepy stomach.
steps: Check your vermicelli packet — if it says “roasted,” skip to step 3. If it’s plain, continue to step 2.

Put the pan on the stove on medium heat with no oil yet. Add the vermicelli and stir constantly with a spoon for about 1 minute, until it turns a shade darker and smells lightly toasty. Tip it out onto a plate and set aside.
In the same pan, add 1 teaspoon of oil and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Add a pinch of mustard seeds. Wait for the popping sound — about 15 seconds.
Add the chopped onion and chilli. Cook for 1 minute, stirring, until the onion softens.

Add a pinch of turmeric and a pinch of salt, then pour in the 1.5 cups of water. Turn the flame up to high and let it come to a full, rolling boil — you’ll see big bubbles across the whole surface, which takes about 2 minutes.
Add the roasted vermicelli, and give it one stir to spread it out evenly in the water.
Cover the pan with a lid, turn the flame down to low, and set a timer for 4 minutes. Don’t lift the lid during this time.
After 4 minutes, remove the lid and fluff gently with a fork — the water should be fully soaked up, with the strands separate rather than sitting in liquid. Serve.
recipes.money_hack: Roasted vermicelli costs slightly more than plain, but saves you the roasting step — worth it if you make this often.
recipes.swap_it: No mustard seeds? Just sauté the onion in oil directly, skipping the tempering step.
recipes.closing_line: Light enough that you won’t regret it by 10am.

recipes.title: Milk Dalia (Broken Wheat Porridge)
recipes.tagline: Warm, mildly sweet, and the kind of breakfast that makes cold mornings bearable.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Dalia cooks into a soft, slightly nutty porridge that’s gentler on the stomach than most breakfast cereals, and it needs almost no attention while it simmers.

ingredients.raw: 1 cup milk (or milk and water mixed)
ingredients.name: milk

steps: Put the dalia and milk into a pan together, right from the start — don’t heat the milk alone first.
Place the pan on the stove and turn the flame to medium.
Watch it closely — milk-based mixtures can rise up fast. The moment you see it starting to rise or bubble at the edges (usually within 2–3 minutes), turn the flame down to low immediately.
Let it simmer gently on low heat for about 8 minutes. Stir every minute — count roughly 60 seconds between each stir — so the dalia doesn’t stick to the bottom.
Watch for the grains to swell up and look plump, and the whole mixture to thicken into a soft, spoonable porridge. That’s your sign it’s nearly done.
Add the sugar and cardamom. Stir well.
Cook for 1 more minute, stirring, until you can’t feel any gritty sugar bits when you taste a small spoonful (careful, it’s hot). Turn off the stove and serve warm.
recipes.money_hack: Dalia is one of the cheapest grains available and keeps for months — a small bag makes many breakfasts.
recipes.swap_it: No milk? Cook it in water instead and stir in a spoon of curd at the end for creaminess.
recipes.closing_line: This is the breakfast equivalent of a soft blanket.

recipes.title: Quick Bread Pakora
recipes.tagline: Crispy, golden, and technically breakfast if you eat it before noon.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: The bread’s absorbent structure soaks up just enough spiced besan batter to crisp beautifully in hot oil without falling apart — a shatteringly crisp coating around a soft, warm centre.
steps: Cut each bread slice diagonally into 2 triangles, so you have 4 triangles total. Set aside.
Put the besan in a bowl. Add the turmeric, chilli powder, and a pinch of salt.
Add water a little at a time — about 2 tablespoons at first — whisking with a fork or spoon after each addition, breaking up any lumps against the side of the bowl.
Keep adding water slowly until you get a smooth batter, about as thick as a milkshake — thin enough to coat the bread but thick enough to actually stick.
Put a pan on the stove, add 2 teaspoons of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Pick up one bread triangle. Dip it fully into the batter, making sure both sides and the crust are coated. Hold it up for a second to let the extra batter drip back into the bowl.
Place it carefully into the hot pan. Repeat with the other triangles, leaving a little space between each one so they’re not touching — this stops them from steaming each other instead of frying.
Let them cook undisturbed for about 2 minutes. Lift one edge with your spatula to check — you want a deep golden-brown colour, not just pale beige.
Flip each one over with your spatula and cook the second side for 2 minutes too, checking the same way.
Once both sides are deep golden, lift them out onto a plate and serve warm.
recipes.money_hack: This is an excellent way to use up bread that’s starting to go a little dry or stale.
recipes.swap_it: No besan? A thin batter of atta with the same spices works as a substitute, though the texture will be slightly different.
recipes.closing_line: Crunchy enough to make you forget it took ten minutes, not thirty.

recipes.title: Cold Veg Sandwich with Mint Chutney
recipes.tagline: Fresh, crunchy, and doesn’t need any cooking or cleanup.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: This leans entirely on freshness and crunch, which makes it the right choice on a warm morning when a hot breakfast feels like the last thing you want.

ingredients.raw: 1 tsp mint or coriander chutney (or ketchup, if that’s what you have)
ingredients.name: mint

steps: Wash the cucumber and carrot under running water for a few seconds.
On a cutting board, slice the cucumber into thin rounds — as thin as you comfortably can, since thick slices make the sandwich hard to bite through.
Slice or grate the carrot the same way.
Lay out 2 slices of bread on a plate. Using a spoon or knife, spread the chutney evenly over both slices, right to the edges — this thin layer helps protect the bread from getting soggy later.
Arrange the cucumber slices evenly over the chutney on one piece of bread.
Add the carrot on top of the cucumber.
Sprinkle a pinch of salt and pepper directly over the vegetables.
Place the second chutney-covered bread slice on top, chutney-side facing down, to close the sandwich.
Press down very gently with your palm, just enough to help it hold together.
Using a knife, cut it in half with one smooth, single cutting motion — don’t saw back and forth, which can push the filling out the sides.
recipes.money_hack: Buy cucumber and carrot in small quantities twice a week rather than a big batch — they lose their crunch quickly once cut.
recipes.swap_it: No chutney on hand? A thin layer of curd mixed with salt and pepper works as a cool, tangy substitute.
recipes.closing_line: Cool, crunchy, and doesn’t ask anything of you before 9am.

recipes.title: Moong Dal Chilla
recipes.tagline: A slightly heartier, protein-packed cousin of the besan chilla.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Soaked and blended moong dal makes a naturally protein-rich batter with a slightly nutty flavour, closer to a savoury dosa than a besan chilla.
steps: First thing — soak the dal. Put ½ cup moong dal in a bowl, cover it completely with water, and leave it for at least 2 hours (or overnight if you’re planning ahead).
When ready to cook, pour the dal into a sieve to drain off the soaking water completely. Give the sieve a shake to remove excess water.
Put the drained dal into a blender, along with the chilli and ginger. Add just a small splash of water — about 2 tablespoons.

Blend for about 30 seconds, then stop and scrape down the sides with a spoon. Blend again for another 20 seconds. Keep repeating this until the batter is completely smooth with no visible dal pieces — it should be thick but pourable, similar to pancake batter.
Pour the batter into a bowl. Add a pinch of salt and the cumin seeds, and stir them in by hand with a spoon (not blended, so they stay whole).
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Pour a ladleful of batter into the centre. Using the back of the ladle, spread it outward in gentle circles from the centre to the edges, making a thin, even circle.
Let it cook undisturbed for about 2 minutes — you’ll see the edges lift slightly and turn golden.
Slide a wide spatula underneath and flip it in one confident motion.
Cook the second side for about 1½ minutes, until golden. Slide onto a plate and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Soak a bigger batch of dal and keep it in the fridge for up to two days — batter can be made fresh each morning without resoaking.
recipes.swap_it: No blender? Finely mash the soaked dal by hand with a fork — it won’t be as smooth, but it still works.
recipes.closing_line: Needs a little planning the night before, but mornings-you will thank tonight-you.

recipes.title: Chai and Rusk (The Classic Combo)
recipes.tagline: Not a recipe so much as a ritual, but it counts as breakfast on the hardest mornings.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Letting the tea leaves actually boil in the water for a minute before the milk goes in is what pulls out real colour and strength, rather than leaving you with pale, weak tea.
steps: Pour 1 cup of water into a small pan. Put it on the stove and turn the flame to high.
Wait until you see big, rolling bubbles across the whole surface — proper boiling, not just steam. This takes about 2–3 minutes.
Add the tea leaves directly into the boiling water. Let them boil, uncovered, for a full 1 minute — don’t add anything else yet, this step is what builds the actual tea flavour.
Add the milk and sugar. Stir once.
Watch the pan closely now, since milk rises fast — bring it back up to a gentle boil, which takes about 1–2 minutes.
The moment it starts to rise, let it simmer for about 2 minutes, watching the colour — you’re looking for a rich, slightly reddish-brown colour, not pale milky beige.
Turn off the stove. Place a small sieve or tea strainer over your cup, and pour the tea through it to catch the leaves.
Take one rusk. Dip it into the hot tea and hold it there for 2–3 seconds — count “one, two, three” — then take it out and eat before it softens too much and breaks. Repeat with each rusk.
recipes.money_hack: A packet of rusks lasts weeks unrefrigerated and costs very little per piece — one of the cheapest ”breakfasts” available.
recipes.swap_it: No milk? Black tea with a little extra sugar works fine too.
recipes.closing_line: Some mornings, this is enough. That’s completely fine.

recipes.title: Curd and Flattened Rice Bowl (Dahi Poha)
recipes.tagline: A cooling, no-cook cousin of regular poha — perfect for warm mornings.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Instead of tempering poha in hot oil, this version simply lets it soften directly in curd — a completely different, cooling experience for a warm morning.
steps: Put the poha in a sieve. Rinse it briefly under running water for about 5 seconds — just a quick pass, not a long soak.
Let it sit in the sieve for 2 minutes. It will soften and turn slightly translucent at the edges on its own.
Tip the softened poha into a bowl.
Add the curd, a pinch of salt, and a pinch of roasted cumin powder.
Using a spoon, fold everything together gently — turn and lift rather than stir hard, since poha strands are delicate and break easily.
If using cucumber or onion, fold it in now, along with the coriander.
Let the bowl sit for 1–2 minutes before eating, if you can spare it — this short rest lets the poha soak up a bit more of the curd’s tang.
recipes.money_hack: This is a great way to use up curd that’s a day or two from its best — the tang actually improves the flavour here.
recipes.swap_it: No roasted cumin powder? Regular cumin powder works, just slightly less smoky in flavour.
recipes.closing_line: Cool, soft, and ready before you’ve even finished waking up.

recipes.title: Dry Garlic Butter Maggi
recipes.tagline: No soupy masala water here — this is Maggi that eats more like a stir-fry.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cutting the water down and finishing the noodles in garlic butter, instead of leaving them swimming in masala liquid, gives you something richer and more concentrated — closer to a proper noodle stir-fry than the bowl-and-spoon experience you’re used to.

ingredients.raw: 1 packet Maggi noodles (use half the tastemaker only)
ingredients.name: maggi noodles

steps: Pour 1 cup of water into a pan — this is less than the usual amount, so keep an eye on it since it heats up faster than you’d expect.
Put the pan on the stove and turn the flame to high. Wait for big, rolling bubbles across the whole surface — that’s a proper boil, about 2 minutes.
Break the noodle block in half with your hands if you want shorter strands, then drop it into the boiling water.

Set a timer for 2 minutes. Stir every 20 seconds with a fork so the noodles don’t clump. Check at the 1-minute mark — because there’s less water this time, it might fully soak up before the timer ends. If the noodles look tender and the water’s mostly gone, stop cooking right there rather than waiting for the full 2 minutes.

Once the noodles are tender and glossy-looking rather than sitting in liquid, sprinkle in half the tastemaker packet and stir it through. Fold the other half of the packet closed and set it aside for another day.
Take a small separate pan. Add the butter and turn the flame to low.
Wait about 30 seconds for the butter to fully melt.
Add the minced garlic. Stir constantly and cook for no more than 30 seconds — the moment you can smell it, that’s your cue, since garlic burns and turns bitter fast if left even a little longer.
Tip the cooked noodles into this garlic butter pan.
Using two forks or a fork and spoon, toss and lift the noodles for about 20 seconds so every strand gets coated in the garlic butter.
Turn off the stove. Sprinkle chilli flakes on top and serve immediately.
recipes.money_hack: Saving half the tastemaker packet each time means one Maggi packet can quietly stretch across two meals.
recipes.swap_it: No butter? A tsp of oil with the garlic works, just slightly less rich.
recipes.closing_line: Same noodles, completely different mood.

recipes.title: Maggi Frittata (Noodle Omelette)
recipes.tagline: What happens when leftover Maggi meets an egg and refuses to be wasted.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Leftover, clumped-together noodles are exactly what lets this hold together as a pancake once bound with egg — crisp outside, soft and savoury in the middle, nothing like soggy reheated noodles.
steps: Crack both eggs into a bowl. Beat with a fork for about 20 seconds until smooth and no white streaks remain.
Add a pinch of salt and pepper, and stir once more.

Add the leftover noodles into the same bowl. Using a fork (or clean fingers), break up any large clumps so the egg can reach every strand, not just the outside of one big lump. This takes about 30 seconds of mixing.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to low-medium — lower than you’d use for a quick omelette, since this needs gentler heat to set all the way through.
Wait 30 seconds for the oil to warm.
Pour the noodle-egg mixture into the pan. Using the back of your spatula, press it down gently into one even, flat layer.
Let it cook completely undisturbed for 3 minutes. Do not touch it. You’ll know it’s ready when the edges look golden and start pulling slightly away from the sides of the pan.

To flip it: slide your spatula all the way underneath to loosen it fully. If you’re not confident flipping it mid-air, instead slide it out onto a plate, then place the pan upside-down over the plate, and quickly flip both together so it drops back into the pan the other way up.
Cook the second side for 2 more minutes, until equally golden.
Slide it onto a plate, cut into wedges if you like, and serve.
recipes.money_hack: This is the single best reason to always cook slightly more Maggi than you think you’ll eat.
recipes.swap_it: No leftover Maggi? Cook a fresh packet with less water than usual to get a similar dry texture.
recipes.closing_line: Leftovers deserve better than the bin, and this proves it.

recipes.title: Peanut Maggi (Dry, Crunchy Twist)
recipes.tagline: A nutty, slightly crunchy variation that tastes nothing like the noodles you’re used to.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Adding crushed peanuts right at the end, off the heat, keeps them properly crunchy against the soft noodles — every bite alternates between the two textures.
steps: Pour the 1 cup of water into a pan and put it on the stove on high heat. Wait for a full, rolling boil — about 2 minutes.

Add the noodles. Set a timer for 2 minutes, stirring every 20 seconds. Check at the 1-minute mark since this smaller amount of water can cook off faster than usual — stop once the noodles are tender and the water is mostly gone.
Stir in the tastemaker while the noodles are still hot, so it dissolves and coats evenly.

While the noodles cook, take a small handful of roasted peanuts and place them on a cutting board or in your palm. Crush them by pressing down firmly with the back of a spoon, or by pressing your palms together with the peanuts in between — you want a mix of larger pieces and small crumbs, not a fine powder.
Once the noodles are done, turn off the stove.
Add the crushed peanuts directly into the pan and toss briefly for about 10 seconds — adding them now, off the heat, keeps them crunchy instead of letting them soften.
Drizzle 1 teaspoon of oil over the top and sprinkle with chilli flakes. Give it one final toss and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Buy peanuts in bulk from a local vendor rather than small packaged bags — much cheaper per handful.
recipes.swap_it: No peanuts? Roasted chana (chickpeas) gives a similar crunch.
recipes.closing_line: Crunchy, nutty, and somehow still ready in eight minutes.

recipes.title: Maggi Bhel
recipes.tagline: Cold, tangy, and probably the most unexpected way to eat instant noodles.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cooled, plain boiled noodles have a firmer, slightly chewy bite that holds up well against raw onion and lemon — completely different from the soft, hot noodles you’re used to.
steps: Boil water in a kettle or pan — enough to fully cover the noodles.

Add the noodles to the boiling water. Do not add the tastemaker packet for this recipe. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring occasionally, until just tender — slightly firmer than you’d normally leave them, since they’ll soften a touch more as they cool.
Drain the noodles in a sieve, shaking off as much water as you can.
Spread the drained noodles out on a plate, rather than leaving them piled in a bowl — this helps them cool faster and stops them clumping together.
Let them sit for about 5 minutes, until they reach room temperature. You can touch them to check — no warmth left.
Transfer the cooled noodles to a bowl. Add the chopped onion and tomato.
Sprinkle a pinch of chaat masala and a pinch of salt over the top.
Cut a lemon in half and squeeze one half over the bowl.
Using your hands or two spoons, toss everything together thoroughly for about 20 seconds, making sure the noodles are evenly coated rather than sitting in clumps with bare noodle showing.
Sprinkle crushed peanuts on top if using, and serve.
recipes.money_hack: This is a smart way to use a Maggi packet whose tastemaker sachet got lost or damaged — you don’t need it here at all.
recipes.swap_it: No lemon? A small splash of vinegar or a dash of tamarind chutney gives similar tang.
recipes.closing_line: Cold noodles, hot weather, perfect match.

recipes.title: Cheesy Maggi (Small Splurge Version)
recipes.tagline: For the day your budget stretches just a little further than usual.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A single processed cheese slice melts smoothly into hot noodles rather than seizing into a rubbery clump — a noticeably creamier, richer version of a food you already know well.
steps: Pour about 1¼ cups of water into a pan — slightly less than the usual 1.5 cups, so the finished sauce ends up a little thicker.
Put the pan on the stove and turn the flame to high. Wait for a full boil, about 2–3 minutes.
Add the noodles and the full tastemaker packet. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring every 20 seconds.
Turn off the stove. The noodles should still be hot and just off the heat.
Take the cheese slice out of its wrapper. Tear it into 4 or 5 smaller pieces with your hands, rather than adding it whole — smaller pieces melt faster and more evenly.
Drop the torn cheese pieces into the hot noodles.

Stir continuously with a fork for about 30 seconds, folding the cheese through until every piece has fully melted and disappeared into a creamy coating — you shouldn’t see any solid cheese pieces left.
Sprinkle chilli flakes on top if you want some heat, and serve immediately — the cheese firms up again as it cools, so eat this one while it’s hot.
recipes.money_hack: Buy cheese slices in a pack rather than a block — you can use exactly one slice per recipe without waste, and the rest keeps in the fridge for weeks.
recipes.swap_it: No cheese? A tablespoon of milk stirred in at the end gives a creamier texture, even without the cheese flavour.
recipes.closing_line: This is the ”treat yourself” recipe of the noodle world.

recipes.title: Maggi Soup Bowl
recipes.tagline: Thinner, brothier, and exactly what you want when you’re coming down with something.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: More water than usual, added deliberately, turns the same familiar tastemaker into a light, warming broth instead of a thick coating sauce — gentler on a sensitive stomach.

ingredients.raw: A few vegetable scraps or frozen peas
ingredients.name: few vegetable scraps

steps: Pour the full 2.5 cups of water into a pan — noticeably more than a standard packet needs, so use a slightly bigger pan if you have one to avoid it boiling over the sides.
Put the pan on the stove and turn the flame to high. Wait for a rolling boil, about 3–4 minutes since there’s extra water this time.
If using vegetables, add them now and let them cook for 1–2 minutes before anything else goes in.
Add the noodles and the tastemaker packet.
Set a timer for 2 minutes, stirring occasionally. Because there’s so much more water, the noodles will float freely rather than sitting in a thick sauce — that’s exactly right.
Turn off the stove. Sprinkle pepper over the top.
Pour into a bowl and eat straight away while it’s properly hot — this recipe loses a lot of its comfort once it cools down.
recipes.money_hack: This is a good way to use vegetable ends and scraps that are too small to cook any other way.
recipes.swap_it: No vegetables at all? Plain is still comforting — this recipe works with just noodles and broth.
recipes.closing_line: For the days your body needs something gentler than usual.

recipes.title: Maggi Fried Rice Style
recipes.tagline: Chopped-up noodles tossed like fried rice — same comfort, different texture entirely.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cutting cooked noodles into shorter pieces before stir-frying changes how they behave in the pan — instead of one long, tangled mass, you get bite-sized pieces that toss more like grains of rice.

ingredients.raw: 1 tsp soy sauce or tomato ketchup
ingredients.name: soy sauce

steps: Boil water in a pan, add the noodles, and cook for 2 minutes without the tastemaker (or use just half if you’d like some flavour).
Drain the noodles in a sieve. Rinse briefly under cool running water for about 5 seconds — this stops the cooking and washes off extra starch so the strands stay separate.

Tip the noodles onto a cutting board. Using kitchen scissors (easiest) or a knife, cut across the noodles into rough 1–2 inch lengths — you don’t need to be precise, just aim for pieces roughly the size of cooked rice grains.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to high. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Add the chopped onion and capsicum. Stir-fry, keeping everything moving constantly, for about 2 minutes until slightly softened but still with some bite.
If using egg: push the vegetables to one side of the pan, crack the egg into the empty space, wait 5 seconds, then scramble it with your spoon for about 20 seconds. Mix it through the vegetables.
Add the chopped noodles and the soy sauce or ketchup.
Toss everything together vigorously on high heat for about 1 minute, using a lifting and turning motion so the sauce coats every piece rather than pooling at the bottom.
Turn off the stove and serve immediately.
recipes.money_hack: This is a great way to use half a leftover Maggi packet alongside whatever small amounts of vegetables are sitting in your fridge.
recipes.swap_it: No soy sauce? Ketchup with a pinch of pepper gives a different but still tasty result.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Maggi — ₹14, Vegetables — ₹4, Sauce — ₹2, Egg (optional) — ₹7. Estimated total — ₹20 (₹27 with egg).
recipes.closing_line: Same noodles, completely different personality.

recipes.title: Tomato Masala Noodles (No Tastemaker)
recipes.tagline: For the day your tastemaker sachet is missing but your noodle craving isn’t.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A properly cooked onion-tomato base does the flavour job the tastemaker packet usually does, and arguably gives you a more rounded taste than the powdered seasoning ever could.
steps: Put a pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Add the chopped onion. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it turns soft and see-through — this is your flavour base, so don’t rush it.

Add the chopped tomato. Cook for 2–3 minutes, pressing down on the pieces gently with the back of your spoon every so often to help them break down. You’ll know it’s ready when the raw tomato smell is gone and it looks soft and saucy rather than firm.
Add a pinch of turmeric, a pinch of chilli powder, and a pinch of salt. Stir for about 30 seconds so the spices cook briefly in the oil rather than tasting raw and powdery.
Pour in the 1.5 cups of water. Turn the flame up to high and wait for a full, rolling boil — about 2–3 minutes.
Add the noodles. Set a timer for 2 minutes, stirring every 20–30 seconds so the masala coats the noodles evenly.
Turn off the stove once the timer’s up, and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Making your own masala base like this means you can use cheaper, plain noodle blocks instead of always buying the branded flavoured packets.
recipes.swap_it: No fresh tomato? A teaspoon of tomato ketchup mixed in works as a decent substitute.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Maggi (noodles only) — ₹10, Vegetables — ₹4, Spices/oil — ₹4. Estimated total — ₹18.
recipes.closing_line: Turns out the tastemaker was never the whole story.

recipes.title: Maggi Upgrade Bowl with Boiled Egg
recipes.tagline: Simple noodles, one boiled egg on top, and suddenly it looks like you tried.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Noodles in a bowl with a halved egg arranged on top look and feel like a meal you planned, even though the only extra step is boiling an egg alongside.

ingredients.raw: Pinch of chilli flakes or pepper
ingredients.name: chilli flakes

steps: Fill a small pan with enough water to fully cover an egg. Put it on the stove and turn the flame to high.
Once it’s boiling (big bubbles across the whole surface), gently lower the egg into the water using a spoon.
Let it boil for 8 minutes for a fully set yolk, or 6–7 minutes if you like the centre a little soft. Set a timer so you don’t lose track.

While the egg cooks, start the noodles in a separate pan: pour in 1.5 cups water, bring to a boil on high heat (about 2–3 minutes), add the noodles and tastemaker, and cook for 2 minutes, stirring occasionally.
When the egg timer goes off, use a spoon to lift the egg out and drop it into a bowl of cold water. Leave it there for 1–2 minutes — this stops the cooking and makes peeling much easier.
Peel the egg: tap it gently all over on a hard surface to crack the shell, then start peeling from the wider end, where there’s usually a small air gap to get your fingernail under.
Once peeled, place the egg on a cutting board. Using a knife, slice it in half lengthwise in one clean cut — wipe the blade with a tissue between cuts if you’re doing more than one egg.
Pour the finished noodles into a bowl. Place the egg halves on top rather than stirring them in.
Sprinkle chilli flakes or pepper over the top and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Boil three or four eggs at once whenever you’re boiling one — extra boiled eggs keep well in the fridge for a few days and upgrade any meal instantly.
recipes.swap_it: No time to boil an egg? A fried egg on top works just as well, and takes less time.
recipes.closing_line: Looks like a proper meal. Took the same ten minutes as always.

recipes.title: Chilli Garlic Noodle Bowl
recipes.tagline: Sharp, spicy, and closer to a street-style noodle stall than a packet of instant noodles.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cooking garlic and chilli briefly in hot oil before the noodles go in releases a sharper, more aromatic flavour that coats every strand instead of just sitting on top.
steps: Boil water in a pan, add the noodles, and cook for 2 minutes. Drain thoroughly in a sieve and set aside — try to move on to the next step fairly soon so they don’t cool and clump.
On a cutting board, peel the garlic cloves and chop them very finely into small bits.
Chop the green chillies finely too — the smaller the pieces, the more evenly the heat spreads through the dish.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium-high. Wait about 30 seconds until the oil looks hot and shimmery.

Add the chopped garlic and chilli together. Stir constantly with your spoon, without stopping, for about 30 seconds — you’re watching for the garlic to turn pale gold at the edges, and listening for a steady sizzle.
The instant the garlic reaches that pale gold colour, add the drained noodles immediately — waiting even a few extra seconds risks burning the garlic and making it bitter.
Add the soy sauce or vinegar.
Toss everything together vigorously on high heat for about 1 minute, lifting and turning constantly so the garlic and chilli spread evenly through the noodles rather than staying clumped in one spot.
Turn off the stove and serve immediately.
recipes.money_hack: Buying garlic as a whole bulb rather than pre-peeled pods is significantly cheaper and lasts for weeks.
recipes.swap_it: No soy sauce or vinegar? A squeeze of lemon at the end adds a similar sharpness.
recipes.closing_line: This one’s got a bit of an attitude. In a good way.

recipes.title: Simple Vegetable Pulao
recipes.tagline: One pot, whatever vegetables you have, and rice that actually tastes like something.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Toasting the rice briefly in oil before any water goes in coats each grain and helps it cook up fluffy and separate rather than sticky.

ingredients.raw: ½ cup mixed vegetables (peas, carrot, beans — whatever you have)
ingredients.name: mixed vegetables

ingredients.raw: 1 bay leaf (optional, if you have whole spices)
ingredients.name: bay leaf

steps: Put the rice in a bowl. Fill it with water, swirl it around with your hand for a few seconds, then carefully pour the cloudy water out while holding the rice back with your fingers. Repeat this 2 more times, until the water you pour out looks mostly clear instead of milky-white. Drain fully.
Put a pot on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium.
If using whole spices, add them now. Wait about 15 seconds — you’ll smell the cinnamon and see the bay leaf curl slightly at the edges.
Add the sliced onion. Cook for about 3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it turns soft and just golden at the edges.
Add the mixed vegetables. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring now and then.
Add the drained rice. Stir gently for about 1 minute, making sure every grain gets coated in the oil — this toasting step is what gives pulao its texture.
Add the 1.5 cups of water and a pinch of salt. Stir once.
Turn the flame up to high and wait for it to reach a full boil — big bubbles across the surface, about 2 minutes.
As soon as it’s boiling, put the lid on tightly and turn the flame down to the lowest setting.
Set a timer for 12 minutes. Do not lift the lid during this time, not even to peek — every peek lets out steam the rice needs.
