When the timer goes off, turn off the stove but leave the lid on. Let it rest undisturbed for 5 more minutes.
Remove the lid. Using a fork, fluff the rice gently by lifting and turning it, rather than stirring hard, so you don’t mash the grains.
recipes.money_hack: Frozen mixed vegetables (if available and affordable) are often cheaper per use than buying several fresh vegetables just for one recipe.
recipes.swap_it: No whole spices? A pinch of garam masala added with the vegetables gives a similar warmth.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rice — ₹8, Vegetables — ₹12, Spices/oil — ₹4, Onion — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹26.
recipes.closing_line: Smells like a proper kitchen. Took twenty minutes and one pot.

recipes.title: Egg Fried Rice
recipes.tagline: The one-pot classic — leftover rice, an egg, and whatever vegetables are lying around.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Rice that’s had time in the fridge has dried out just enough to fry up separate and slightly crisp, instead of clumping into a sticky mass the way fresh rice would.

ingredients.raw: 1.5 cups cooked rice (a day old works best)
ingredients.name: cooked rice

steps: Take the cold rice and break up any large clumps with your fingers or a fork before it goes near the pan — this is much easier to do now than once it’s hot in the pan.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to high. Wait about 30 seconds until the oil looks hot and shimmery.
Add the chopped onion and capsicum. Stir-fry, keeping everything moving, for about 1 minute.
Push the vegetables over to one side of the pan with your spatula, creating an empty space on the other side.
Crack the egg into that empty space. Wait 5 seconds, then scramble it with the edge of your spatula for about 20 seconds.
Mix the scrambled egg through the vegetables.
Add the rice. Using a folding and tossing motion — lifting from the bottom and turning it over, rather than stirring in circles — mix everything together for about 30 seconds.
Add the soy sauce, pepper, and salt.
Continue tossing on high heat for about 2 minutes. You’re looking for a few grains to pick up a light golden colour where they touch the hot pan directly.
Turn off the stove and serve immediately.
recipes.money_hack: Day-old rice fries much better than fresh — it’s drier and doesn’t turn mushy. Worth deliberately cooking extra rice the night before.
recipes.swap_it: No soy sauce? A dash of vinegar and a little extra salt gets you close.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rice (leftover) — ₹6, Egg — ₹7, Vegetables — ₹4, Sauce/oil — ₹3. Estimated total — ₹20.
recipes.closing_line: Leftover rice’s best possible future.

recipes.title: South Indian Lemon Rice
recipes.tagline: Tangy, light, and needs almost no vegetables to taste complete.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Frying mustard seeds briefly in hot oil releases far more flavour than sprinkling them in raw — that flavoured oil then coats the rice, and the fresh lemon juice at the end makes it taste bright and finished.
steps: If your rice is piping hot, let it sit for a few minutes to cool slightly — hot rice breaks apart and turns mushy when tossed, while slightly cooled rice holds its shape.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Add a pinch of mustard seeds. Wait for them to pop — a clear crackling sound, about 15 seconds.
Add the chilli and peanuts if using. Cook for about 1 minute, until the peanuts turn a shade darker.
Add a pinch of turmeric. Stir for just a few seconds — long enough to see the oil turn yellow, not long enough to let it sit and taste raw.
Add the cooked rice. Using a folding motion — turning gently from underneath rather than stirring hard — mix it through the tempering so the yellow colour spreads evenly.
Turn off the stove completely before the next step — this matters, since cooking lemon juice even briefly dulls its brightness.
Cut the lemon in half. Squeeze both halves over the rice. Add a pinch of salt.
Toss well, then taste a small spoonful (careful, it may still be warm) — add a touch more lemon or salt if it needs it.
recipes.money_hack: This is a great way to use rice that’s slightly dried out from sitting in the fridge — the lemon and tempering bring it back to life.
recipes.swap_it: No mustard seeds? Cumin seeds work as a substitute in the tempering.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rice — ₹6, Lemon — ₹3, Peanuts — ₹3, Spices/oil — ₹4. Estimated total — ₹16.
recipes.closing_line: Tangy enough to wake up even the most tired taste buds.

recipes.title: One-Pot Tomato Rice
recipes.tagline: Rich, slightly tangy, and cooks entirely in one pot with almost no supervision.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cooking rice directly in a tomato-onion base means every grain absorbs that flavour as it swells and softens, rather than just having sauce sitting on top.
steps: Rinse the rice: fill the bowl with water, swirl, pour out the cloudy water while holding the rice back, and repeat 2–3 times until the water runs clear. Drain fully.
Put a pot on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook for 2–3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent.

Add the chopped tomatoes. Cook for 4–5 minutes, pressing them gently with the back of your spoon every minute or so to help them break down. You’re watching for the pieces to lose their firm shape and turn into a soft, jammy mass, with a little oil visible at the edges — that’s your sign the raw tomato taste is gone.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, and salt. Stir for about 1 minute.
Add the drained rice and stir well so every grain gets coated in the tomato base.
Add the 1.5 cups of water and stir once more.
Turn the flame up to high and wait for a full boil, about 2 minutes.
Cover tightly with a lid and reduce the flame to the lowest setting. Set a timer for 12 minutes. Don’t lift the lid during this time.
When the timer goes off, turn off the stove and let it rest, covered, for 5 more minutes.
Remove the lid and fluff gently with a fork before serving.
recipes.money_hack: This is one of the best uses for tomatoes that have gone a bit too soft to eat raw.
recipes.swap_it: No fresh tomatoes? Two tablespoons of tomato purée or ketchup mixed with a little water works as a substitute.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rice — ₹8, Tomatoes — ₹6, Onion — ₹2, Spices/oil — ₹4. Estimated total — ₹20.
recipes.closing_line: One pot, minimal effort, maximum comfort.

recipes.title: Comfort Khichdi
recipes.tagline: Rice and dal cooked together into one soft, warm, everything-is-okay-now bowl.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Khichdi wants the rice and dal to fully merge into a soft, porridge-like texture, which is why the water quantity here is deliberately higher and the cooking time longer than a typical rice dish.

ingredients.raw: ¼ cup yellow moong dal or toor dal
ingredients.name: yellow moong dal

steps: Rinse the rice and dal together in a bowl: fill with water, swirl, pour out the cloudy water while holding everything back with your fingers, repeat 2 times until it runs mostly clear.
Put a pot on the stove, add the ghee, and turn the flame to medium. Wait about 20 seconds for it to melt.
Add the cumin seeds. Wait for them to sizzle — about 10 seconds.
Add the rinsed rice and dal together. Stir for about 1 minute so both are lightly coated in the ghee — you’ll notice a faint nutty smell starting.
Add a pinch of turmeric, a pinch of salt, and the full 2.5 cups of water.
Turn the flame up to high and bring it to a boil — about 3 minutes.
Once boiling, turn the flame down to a gentle simmer (low-medium) and cover the pot partially — leave a small gap for steam to escape, don’t seal it completely like you would for plain rice.
Set a timer for 18 minutes. Stir every 3–4 minutes with a spoon so nothing sticks to the bottom.

Check at the 18-minute mark: the rice and dal should have both softened completely and lost their separate shapes, and the whole mixture should look thick but still easy to spoon — almost like a savoury porridge.
If it’s thicker than you’d like, stir in a small splash of hot water. Turn off the stove and serve warm.
recipes.money_hack: Cook a bigger batch — khichdi reheats well the next day with a splash of water stirred in.
recipes.swap_it: No dal on hand? Plain rice porridge with just cumin and salt is still soothing, if less protein-rich.
recipes.closing_line: This is what being taken care of tastes like.

recipes.title: Simple Peas Pulao
recipes.tagline: Sweet peas, fragrant rice, and barely any effort involved.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Peas are naturally sweet, and cooking them briefly in ghee before the rice goes in brings that sweetness out even more.
steps: Rinse the rice in a bowl: fill with water, swirl, pour off the cloudy water while holding the rice back, repeat 2–3 times until it runs clear. Drain fully.
Put a pot on the stove, add the ghee, and turn the flame to medium.
If using whole spices, add them now and wait about 10 seconds until fragrant.
Add the peas — if frozen, no need to thaw first, just tip them straight in. Cook for about 1 minute, stirring, just to take the raw edge off.
Add the drained rice. Stir for about 1 minute so it’s evenly coated in the ghee.
Add the water and a pinch of salt. Stir once.
Turn the flame up to high and bring to a full boil — about 2 minutes.
Cover tightly with a lid and turn the flame down to the lowest setting. Set a timer for 12 minutes. Don’t lift the lid.
When the timer goes off, turn off the stove and let it sit, still covered, for 5 more minutes.
Remove the lid and fluff gently with a fork, being careful not to mash the peas.
recipes.money_hack: Frozen peas are available cheaply year-round and don’t need peeling — a small bag lasts many meals.
recipes.swap_it: No whole spices? A pinch of garam masala works as a simpler substitute.
recipes.closing_line: Sweet, soft, and quietly one of the easiest things you’ll ever cook.

recipes.title: Quick Rajma Rice
recipes.tagline: A simplified take on the North Indian classic, using boiled or canned kidney beans.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Starting with already-boiled rajma means all your time goes into building a proper masala base rather than waiting for beans to soften.

ingredients.raw: 1 cup boiled rajma (kidney beans) — home-cooked or canned
ingredients.name: boiled rajma

steps: Put a pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook for about 4 minutes, stirring occasionally — you want it to turn properly golden-brown, not just soft, since that deeper colour gives the gravy more flavour.
Add the chopped tomato. Cook for 3–4 minutes, mashing gently with your spoon, until it fully breaks down into a soft, jammy texture with no firm pieces left.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, garam masala, and salt. Stir for about 1 minute.
Add the boiled rajma along with a small splash of water — enough to loosen everything into a gravy, not a dry sauté.
Turn the flame down to low-medium and let it simmer for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Partway through, press a few beans gently against the side of the pan with the back of your spoon — this releases starch and naturally thickens the gravy.
Turn off the stove once the gravy looks thick and well combined. Serve hot, ladled generously over rice.
recipes.money_hack: Boil a large batch of rajma on a free afternoon (soak overnight, pressure cook or boil until soft) and freeze in portions — this turns a slow dish into a 15-minute one anytime.
recipes.swap_it: No rajma? Boiled chickpeas or even boiled black-eyed peas work with the same masala base.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rajma (boiled) — ₹12, Vegetables — ₹5, Spices/oil — ₹4, Rice — ₹5. Estimated total — ₹26.
recipes.closing_line: All the comfort of a slow-cooked dish, none of the actual waiting.

recipes.title: Chana Masala Rice Bowl
recipes.tagline: Spiced chickpeas over rice — filling, protein-rich, and genuinely tasty.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Chickpeas hold their shape a little more firmly than kidney beans, giving you distinct chunks in every spoonful rather than a fully merged gravy.
steps: Put a pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook for about 4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it turns a proper deep gold colour.
Add the chopped tomato. Cook for 3–4 minutes, mashing gently against the pan as it cooks, until it turns soft and glossy with no firm pieces left.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, garam masala, and salt. Stir for about 1 minute.
Add the boiled chickpeas along with a small splash of water.
Turn the flame down and let it simmer gently for about 8 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Partway through, press a few chickpeas gently against the side of the pan with your spoon — this thickens the gravy naturally.
Turn off the stove once thick and well combined. Serve hot over rice.
recipes.money_hack: Chickpeas are one of the cheapest protein sources available — buying dried chickpeas and boiling your own works out far cheaper than canned.
recipes.swap_it: No garam masala? A pinch of cumin powder and coriander powder makes a reasonable substitute blend.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Chickpeas (boiled) — ₹10, Vegetables — ₹5, Spices/oil — ₹4, Rice — ₹5. Estimated total — ₹24.
recipes.closing_line: Filling enough to make you forget how little it cost.

recipes.title: Budget Schezwan Fried Rice
recipes.tagline: A milder, cheaper take on the spicy Indo-Chinese favourite.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cooking garlic hot and fast, right at the start, recreates the sharp, tangy heat of real Schezwan sauce using nothing more exotic than pantry basics.

ingredients.raw: ½ tsp chilli sauce or chilli powder
ingredients.name: chilli sauce

steps: Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to high. Wait about 30 seconds until the oil looks hot and shimmery — hotter than most other rice recipes in this book.

Add the chopped garlic alone first. Stir constantly, without stopping, for 20–30 seconds — watch for it to turn pale gold and smell fragrant. Pull it off that heat level immediately once it does; another few seconds and it burns.
Add the chopped onion and capsicum right away. Stir-fry, keeping everything moving, for about 1 minute.
Add the rice, breaking up any clumps as you mix it in.
Add the ketchup, chilli sauce, and soy sauce.

Toss everything together vigorously on high heat for about 2 minutes — you’re looking for the rice to pick up an even reddish tint and a few grains to show light charring where they touch the pan directly.
Turn off the stove and serve immediately.
recipes.money_hack: Small sachets of chilli sauce or ketchup (the kind that come with delivery orders) are perfect for recipes like this — save them instead of throwing them away.
recipes.swap_it: No chilli sauce? A pinch of dried red chilli flakes mixed into the ketchup gets you close.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rice — ₹6, Vegetables — ₹4, Garlic — ₹2, Sauces/oil — ₹5. Estimated total — ₹17.
recipes.closing_line: Cheaper than delivery, spicier than you expected.

recipes.title: Curry Leaf & Peanut Rice
recipes.tagline: A South Indian-style rice that’s fragrant, nutty, and needs very few ingredients.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Curry leaves release almost all of their fragrance the moment they hit hot oil — a few seconds of sizzling unlocks a smell raw curry leaves simply don’t have.

ingredients.raw: A small handful curry leaves (fresh, if you can find them)
ingredients.name: small handful curry leaves

steps: Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Add a pinch of mustard seeds. Wait for the popping and crackling sound — about 10–15 seconds.
Add the curry leaves right away — they’ll sizzle loudly and might spit a little, so stand back slightly if needed, that’s completely normal.
Add the peanuts at the same time. Cook for about 1 minute, until the peanuts turn a shade darker and the curry leaves look slightly crisp.
Add a pinch of turmeric. Stir for just a few seconds to let its colour bloom in the hot oil.
Add the cooked rice. Using a folding motion — turning gently from underneath — mix it through so the tempering distributes evenly without crushing the peanuts or curry leaves.
Add salt to taste, toss once more, and serve while still warm.
recipes.money_hack: Dried curry leaves (sold in small packets) work almost as well as fresh and last much longer without going bad.
recipes.swap_it: No curry leaves at all? Skip them — the mustard seeds and peanuts still give a good tempering flavour on their own.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rice — ₹6, Peanuts — ₹4, Curry leaves/spices — ₹4. Estimated total — ₹14.
recipes.closing_line: Simple ingredients, but the smell alone makes it feel special.

recipes.title: Budget Paneer Pulao
recipes.tagline: A small amount of paneer goes a long way when it’s tucked into a full pot of rice.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Frying the paneer briefly before it goes anywhere near the rice gives it a light golden crust that holds its texture rather than turning soft and forgettable once mixed in.

ingredients.raw: ½ cup peas or mixed vegetables
ingredients.name: peas

steps: Cut the paneer into small cubes, about the size of a dice, using a knife on a cutting board.
Rinse the rice: fill with water, swirl, pour off the cloudy water while holding the rice back, repeat 2–3 times until it runs clear. Drain.
Put a pot on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium.
Add the paneer cubes in a single layer, spread apart so they’re not touching. Let them sit undisturbed for 45 seconds — don’t move them yet, this is what gives them a proper golden crust.
Turn each cube over with a spoon and let the other side cook for another 30–40 seconds, until lightly golden. Remove the paneer to a plate and set aside.
In the same pot (no need to clean it — the browned bits add flavour), add the onion. Cook for about 2 minutes until soft.
Add the peas and cook for 1 minute.
Add the drained rice, garam masala, and a pinch of salt. Stir for about 1 minute to coat the rice in the remaining oil and spice.
Add the water, stir once, and turn the flame up to high. Wait for a full boil, about 2 minutes.
Cover tightly and turn the flame down to the lowest setting. Set a timer for 12 minutes. Don’t lift the lid.

At the 10-minute mark of the timer, quickly lift the lid, scatter the fried paneer over the top of the rice, and re-cover immediately — this lets the paneer warm through gently in the last 2 minutes of steam rather than cooking further and toughening.
When the timer ends, turn off the stove and let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes before fluffing gently with a fork.
recipes.money_hack: Buy paneer in the smallest pack available (100g) if you’re only using it occasionally — it doesn’t keep well once opened, so there’s no benefit to buying more than you’ll use soon.
recipes.swap_it: No paneer? Boiled, cubed potato makes a different but still satisfying version.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rice — ₹8, Paneer — ₹16, Vegetables — ₹5, Spices/oil — ₹4. Estimated total — ₹33.
recipes.closing_line: A little paneer, spread across a whole pot, still feels like a treat.

recipes.title: Egg Curry Rice Bowl
recipes.tagline: Boiled eggs simmered in a simple tomato-onion gravy, served over rice.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Once boiled and simmered briefly in a proper masala gravy, eggs take on flavour the way meat would in a similar curry, cooking in a fraction of the time.
steps: If you haven’t already boiled your eggs: place them in a small pan of water, bring to a boil on high heat, then boil for 8–9 minutes. Transfer to a bowl of cold water for 2 minutes, then peel.
Put a pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook for about 4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until deep golden-brown — don’t rush this step, since a well-browned onion is most of what gives this simple gravy real depth.
Add the chopped tomato. Cook for 3–4 minutes, mashing gently, until it fully breaks down into a soft, glossy mixture.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, garam masala, and salt. Stir for about 1 minute.
Add a small splash of water to loosen the mixture into a gravy, and let it simmer for 3–4 minutes.
Using a knife, halve the boiled eggs lengthwise — wipe the blade with a tissue between cuts if doing more than one, to keep the yolk from smearing.
Nestle the egg halves into the gravy, cut-side up, and spoon a little sauce over the yolks.
Let them warm through gently for 1–2 minutes without stirring vigorously, which can break the yolks apart and cloud the gravy.
Turn off the stove and serve over rice.
recipes.money_hack: Boiling four eggs instead of two, and saving the extras for another recipe, saves you from heating water twice in one day.
recipes.swap_it: No garam masala? A pinch each of cumin and coriander powder makes a decent substitute.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Eggs — ₹14, Vegetables — ₹5, Spices/oil — ₹4, Rice — ₹5. Estimated total — ₹28.
recipes.closing_line: Saucy, warm, and a genuinely good reason to boil an extra egg.

recipes.title: Masala Rice with Roasted Papad
recipes.tagline: Simple spiced rice, made complete with the crunch of a roasted papad on the side.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A crisp, freshly roasted papad adds a completely different texture and a toasty aroma that turns “just rice” into something that feels properly finished.
steps: Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook for about 2 minutes, until soft.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, and salt. Stir for a few seconds.
Add the cooked rice and toss well, folding it through the spice mix until every grain looks evenly coated and warmed through — about 1 minute.
Turn off the stove and set the rice aside, covered, to keep it warm.

To roast the papad over an open flame: hold it with tongs about an inch above the flame, and keep turning it constantly and evenly. You’re watching for it to puff up slightly and darken evenly in small spots — this takes about 15–20 seconds per side.

If using a dry pan instead: put it on medium heat, place the papad in, and press it down firmly and evenly with a spatula, flipping every few seconds so it doesn’t scorch in one spot before the rest crisps.
Once evenly roasted (it should look puffed and feel crisp, not floppy), serve the rice hot with the papad on the side, or crumble it over the top.
recipes.money_hack: A packet of papads lasts a long time and costs very little per piece — always worth keeping a few on hand.
recipes.swap_it: No papad? A few crushed plain crackers on top gives a similar crunch.
recipes.closing_line: One crunchy papad can save an otherwise boring bowl of rice.

recipes.title: Simple Dal-Chawal
recipes.tagline: Rice and dal, served separately rather than cooked together — the other great Indian comfort combination.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: The tempering poured over the finished dal at the end is what elevates this from “boiled lentils” to something genuinely craveable — don’t skip that final step even when you’re tired.

ingredients.raw: ¼ cup toor or moong dal
ingredients.name: toor

steps: Rinse the rice in a small pan: fill with water, swirl, pour off the cloudy water, repeat once or twice. Add the 1 cup of fresh water, put it on the stove on high heat, and bring to a boil, about 2 minutes.
Once boiling, cover, turn the flame down to low, and let it simmer for 12 minutes. Then turn off the heat and leave it covered to stay warm — set this pan aside.
In a separate pot, rinse the dal the same way. Add the 2.5 cups of water and a pinch of turmeric.
Put this pot on the stove on high heat and bring it to a boil, about 3 minutes.
Turn the flame down to a simmer. Cook for about 15 minutes, mashing gently with the back of your spoon every few minutes — you’re aiming for it to break down into a slightly thick, soupy consistency.
While the dal simmers, make the tempering: heat the ghee in a small separate pan on medium heat, add the cumin seeds, and wait about 10 seconds for them to sizzle.
Add the chopped onion and tomato to the tempering pan. Cook for about 2 minutes, until soft.

Once the dal has reached the consistency you want, pour the hot tempering (onion, tomato, and all the ghee) directly into the dal pot — it will sizzle loudly on contact, which is exactly right, that sizzle releases the aroma straight into the dal.
Add salt to taste, stir once, and serve the dal hot, ladled generously over the warm rice.
recipes.money_hack: Cook a bigger batch of dal — it keeps for a couple of days in the fridge and reheats well with a splash of water.
recipes.swap_it: No fresh tomato? Skip it — a simple cumin-onion tempering is still deeply comforting on its own.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rice — ₹5, Dal — ₹6, Vegetables/spices — ₹5, Ghee — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹18.
recipes.closing_line: This is the meal that quietly fixes a bad day.

recipes.title: Carrot & Coconut Rice
recipes.tagline: A lightly sweet, fragrant rice dish that feels a little different from the usual.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Grating the carrot means it cooks through almost instantly and blends seamlessly into the rice, giving you a soft, evenly sweet character throughout rather than occasional sweet bites.

ingredients.raw: 1 tbsp desiccated coconut (or fresh, if available)
ingredients.name: desiccated coconut

steps: Wash the carrot under running water. Using a grater, grate it on a plate — hold the carrot firmly against the grater and move it up and down until it’s fully shredded.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Add a pinch of mustard seeds. Wait for the popping sound, about 10–15 seconds.
Add the grated carrot. Cook for about 2 minutes, stirring frequently, until it softens and turns slightly translucent at the edges rather than staying raw and firm.
Add the cooked rice, the coconut, and a pinch of salt.
Using a folding motion, toss everything together gently for about 1 minute, making sure the carrot and coconut spread evenly rather than clumping in one spot.
Cook for 1 more minute just to warm everything through evenly, then turn off the stove and serve while still warm.
recipes.money_hack: A small packet of desiccated coconut lasts a long time in the pantry and works in both sweet and savoury recipes.
recipes.swap_it: No coconut? Skip it — the carrot and tempering alone still make a nice, lightly sweet rice dish.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Rice — ₹6, Carrot — ₹4, Coconut — ₹4, Spices/oil — ₹3. Estimated total — ₹17.
recipes.closing_line: A little different, a little sweet, still done in fifteen minutes.

recipes.title: Roti Pizza
recipes.tagline: Leftover roti, whatever toppings you’ve got, and a hot pan — that’s the whole recipe.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A covered pan traps enough heat and steam to melt the cheese and soften the vegetables at the same time — without the lid, the top stays cold while the bottom risks burning.

ingredients.raw: 1 cheese slice or a sprinkle of grated cheese (optional)
ingredients.name: cheese slice

ingredients.raw: Pinch of oregano or chilli flakes
ingredients.name: oregano

steps: Lay the roti flat on a plate. Using a spoon, spread the ketchup or chutney over it in a thin, even layer, right to the edges.
On a cutting board, slice the onion and capsicum as thinly as you can manage.
Scatter the sliced onion and capsicum evenly over the sauce-covered roti.
If using cheese, place the slice on top now, or sprinkle the grated cheese evenly across the surface.
Put a dry pan on the stove and turn the flame to low — lower than usual, since anything higher will burn the base before the toppings soften.
Carefully slide the topped roti into the pan.
Cover immediately with a lid. Set a timer for 3 minutes and don’t lift the lid during this time — the trapped steam is doing the cooking.
After 3 minutes, lift the lid and check: the cheese should look fully melted and the vegetables slightly softened. If not quite there, cover again and cook for 1 more minute.
Turn off the stove. Using a spatula, slide the pizza out onto a plate. While it’s still hot, sprinkle oregano or chilli flakes on top. Cut into wedges and eat.
recipes.money_hack: This is the best possible use for a roti that’s gone a little too dry to eat plain.
recipes.swap_it: No cheese? A well-seasoned topping of vegetables and chutney is still tasty without it.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Roti — ₹5, Toppings — ₹8, Cheese (optional) — ₹8. Estimated total — ₹13 (₹21 with cheese).
recipes.closing_line: Pizza logic, roti budget.

recipes.title: Vegetable Roti Roll
recipes.tagline: Stir-fried vegetables wrapped in a warm roti — portable, filling, and endlessly customisable.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cooking the vegetables until any extra moisture has cooked away is what keeps the roti from getting soggy — a wet filling seeps in and makes it fall apart within minutes.
steps: On a cutting board, slice the onion, capsicum, and carrot thinly, trying to keep all the pieces roughly the same size so they cook evenly together.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium-high. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.

Add all the sliced vegetables together. Stir-fry constantly, keeping them moving, for 3–4 minutes — you’re watching for them to soften while still holding a slight bite, with any liquid in the pan mostly cooked away by the time you finish.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, and salt. Toss to coat evenly, then turn off the stove.

Take the roti. Warm it by holding it directly over a low flame for a few seconds on each side using tongs, turning until it feels soft and bendy. (No open flame? Warm it in a dry pan for about 20 seconds per side instead.)
Lay the warm roti flat. Using a spoon, spread the chutney or ketchup down the centre.
Pile the cooked vegetables on top of the chutney, in a line down the middle rather than spread edge to edge.
Fold the bottom edge of the roti up and over the filling first.
Continue rolling from one side to the other, tucking in tightly as you go so nothing spills out the ends.
recipes.money_hack: This recipe is a great way to use up small leftover bits of several vegetables that aren’t individually enough for a full dish.
recipes.swap_it: No fresh vegetables? Leftover bhurji or dal also rolls up well in a roti.
recipes.closing_line: Handheld, filling, and doesn’t require sitting still to eat.

recipes.title: Sweet Coconut Stuffed Roti
recipes.tagline: A simple, lightly sweet stuffed flatbread for when you want something a little different.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Not overfilling the dough and sealing the edges firmly before rolling is what stops the jaggery from bursting through while you roll it out.
steps: Put the atta in a bowl. Add water a little at a time — about 1 tablespoon at a time — kneading with both hands between each addition, until you get a soft, smooth dough. This dough should feel slightly softer than usual roti dough.
Cover the bowl with a plate or cloth and let it rest for 5 minutes — this relaxes the dough and makes rolling easier later.
While it rests, make the filling: put the coconut, jaggery (grated or crushed finely), and cardamom into a small bowl. Mix well with a spoon until combined.
Divide the rested dough into 2 balls, slightly larger than you’d make for a plain roti.
Take one ball. Flatten it in your palm into a small disc, about the size of your palm.
Place about 1 tablespoon of the coconut-jaggery filling in the centre — don’t overfill, since too much filling makes sealing difficult.
Bring the edges of the dough up and over the filling, gathering them together at the top like a small pouch, and pinch them firmly together to seal completely, with no gaps.

Gently flatten the sealed ball with your palm, then using a rolling pin, roll it out carefully — apply light, even pressure, and stop immediately if you feel resistance or see the filling starting to poke through.
Put your tawa on the stove and turn the flame to medium. Wait about 1 minute for it to heat.
Place the rolled roti on the tawa. Watch closely — if you see any dark, wet patches forming, that’s leaking jaggery, so move the roti to a slightly cooler part of the pan.
Cook for about 2 minutes, add a little ghee, flip, add ghee to the other side, and cook for 2 more minutes, until golden-brown spots appear on both sides. Repeat steps 5–11 with the second ball.
recipes.money_hack: This filling also works well as a spread on plain bread if you don’t want to make dough at all.
recipes.swap_it: No jaggery? Sugar works, though jaggery gives a deeper, more caramel-like flavour.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Atta — ₹6, Coconut — ₹5, Jaggery — ₹3, Ghee — ₹4. Estimated total — ₹18.
recipes.closing_line: Sweet enough to feel like dessert, simple enough to make on a Tuesday.

recipes.title: Crispy Roti Chips with Chutney
recipes.tagline: Leftover roti, cut up and fried crisp — a snack that costs almost nothing.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Dry, slightly hard roti fries up better than soft, fresh roti — there’s less moisture inside to fight against, so it crisps properly instead of turning greasy and limp.

ingredients.raw: Pinch of chaat masala or salt
ingredients.name: chaat masala

steps: Put each roti flat on a cutting board. Using a knife, cut it into 4–6 triangles, trying to keep them roughly even in size.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds until it looks shimmery.
Place the roti triangles into the pan in a single layer, without them overlapping — if they don’t all fit, fry in two batches rather than crowding the pan.
Let them fry for about 2 minutes. Check the underside by lifting one with your spatula — you want an even golden-brown colour.
Flip each piece over and fry the second side for another 2 minutes, checking the same way.
Once both sides are golden and you notice the sizzling sound has become a little quieter, remove them from the pan onto a plate.
While still hot, sprinkle chaat masala or salt over them — seasoning sticks much better to hot, slightly oily chips.
Serve immediately with ketchup or chutney for dipping.
recipes.money_hack: This is specifically designed for rotis that have gone hard or dry — don’t throw those away, this is exactly what they’re for.
recipes.swap_it: No chaat masala? Plain salt and a squeeze of lemon works just as well.
recipes.closing_line: Turns ”this roti is too dry to eat” into an actual snack.

recipes.title: Curd Roti Wrap
recipes.tagline: A cool, tangy wrap that needs no cooking beyond warming the roti.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Whisking the curd thoroughly before spreading it is what turns lumpy, watery curd into something smooth that spreads and stays evenly distributed once rolled.
steps: Put the curd into a bowl. Using a fork or small whisk, whisk it vigorously for about 30 seconds — keep going until it looks smooth and slightly loose, with no lumps remaining.
If you’d like the roti soft and warm, warm it now by holding it over a low flame for a few seconds on each side, or in a dry pan for about 20 seconds per side.
Lay the roti flat. Using a spoon, spread the whisked curd evenly over it, leaving a small bare border around the edge so it doesn’t squeeze out once rolled.
Finely chop the cucumber or onion on a cutting board, and scatter it evenly over the curd.
Sprinkle a pinch of chaat masala and a pinch of salt over the top.
Starting from one edge, roll the roti up firmly and tightly, rather than loosely, so it holds together when you pick it up.
recipes.money_hack: This is a good way to use curd that’s slightly more sour than you’d want to eat plain — the tang works well here.
recipes.swap_it: No cucumber? Grated carrot or thinly sliced onion both work well instead.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Roti — ₹5, Curd — ₹8, Vegetables — ₹2, Masala — ₹1. Estimated total — ₹16.
recipes.closing_line: Cool, tangy, and barely counts as cooking.

recipes.title: Simple Missi Roti
recipes.tagline: A spiced, besan-enriched roti that’s a little more flavourful than the everyday kind.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Besan doesn’t develop gluten the way wheat flour does, so this roti ends up slightly more crumbly and rustic, with a deeper, nuttier flavour from the gram flour mixed directly into the dough.

ingredients.raw: Pinch of carom seeds (ajwain) or cumin seeds
ingredients.name: carom seeds

steps: Put the atta and besan together in a bowl. Mix them together dry with your hand or a spoon first, before adding anything wet.
Add the chopped onion, carom seeds, chilli powder, and a pinch of salt. Mix through the dry flour.

Add water gradually, about 1 tablespoon at a time, kneading with both hands between each addition. This dough often needs a bit more water than plain atta dough, so don’t be surprised if it takes 5–6 tablespoons total to reach a firm, smooth consistency.
Divide the dough into 2 balls.

Take one ball and roll it out on a lightly floured surface, using gentle, even pressure and rotating the dough often — this dough can tear more easily than plain wheat dough at the edges, so go slowly.
Put your tawa on the stove and turn the flame to medium. Wait about 1 minute for it to heat.
Place the rolled roti on the tawa. Cook for about 1 minute, then flip.
Add a little oil, spreading it with the back of your spoon, and press gently around the edges with your spatula. Cook for 2 minutes.
Flip again, add oil to this side too, and cook for 1–2 more minutes, until golden-brown spots appear on both sides. Repeat with the second ball.
recipes.money_hack: This roti is filling enough to eat with just a smear of butter or pickle, saving you the cost of making a separate side dish.
recipes.swap_it: No carom seeds? Cumin seeds or a pinch of dried fenugreek leaves work as substitutes.
recipes.closing_line: Flavourful enough to skip the side dish entirely.

recipes.title: Stovetop Cheese Garlic Roti
recipes.tagline: No tandoor, no oven — just a roti, garlic butter, and a hot pan doing all the work.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Covering the pan while the cheese melts traps enough heat above to soften it while the pan crisps the base below — the same trick as the roti pizza.

ingredients.raw: 1 roti or chapati (fresh, uncooked dough works best if you have it)
ingredients.name: roti

ingredients.raw: 1 tbsp grated cheese or 1 cheese slice
ingredients.name: grated cheese

steps: Peel and finely chop the garlic clove on a cutting board.
Put the butter in a small bowl. Add the chopped garlic and mix thoroughly with a spoon so it’s evenly spread through, not sitting in one clump.
Warm the roti briefly in a dry pan, about 20 seconds per side, until soft and bendable.
Using a knife, spread the garlic butter generously over one side of the roti, right to the edges.
If using a cheese slice, tear it into small, even pieces with your hands rather than leaving it whole — smaller pieces melt faster. Scatter the cheese evenly over the buttered roti.
Cover the pan with a lid, and turn the flame to low.
Cook for about 1 minute, checking once — you’re waiting for the cheese to fully melt and turn glossy, not just soften at the edges.
Turn off the stove, sprinkle coriander on top if using, and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Buying garlic as a whole bulb and butter in a small block, rather than pre-made garlic butter, works out much cheaper across many recipes.
recipes.swap_it: No cheese? Garlic butter roti is still genuinely tasty on its own.
recipes.closing_line: Restaurant naan vibes, hostel-room budget.

recipes.title: Bread Uttapam
recipes.tagline: A thicker, pancake-style breakfast using torn bread instead of a fermented batter.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Soaking the bread fully and then squeezing out the water is what turns it into a sticky, mouldable mixture that holds its shape in the pan, rather than a loose, crumbly mess.
steps: Tear the bread slices into small pieces with your hands and drop them into a bowl of water, pressing down gently so they’re fully submerged.
Let them soak for about 30 seconds — just long enough to fully soften, not so long they start dissolving.
Lift the bread out with your hands and squeeze it firmly over the sink, pressing out as much water as you can.
Put the squeezed bread in a bowl. Using a fork, mash it until it forms a rough, sticky, combined mixture rather than distinct wet chunks.
Add the onion, tomato, a pinch of turmeric, and a pinch of salt. Mix thoroughly so everything is evenly distributed.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Spoon the bread mixture into the pan and spread it out with the back of your spoon into a flat, even disc about a centimetre thick.
Let it cook undisturbed for about 3 minutes — you’re waiting for the underside to turn golden and firm enough to flip cleanly.
Slide a wide spatula underneath and flip it carefully.
Cook the second side for 2–3 minutes, then remove and serve.
recipes.money_hack: This works particularly well with bread that’s gone slightly stale, since it needs to be soaked anyway.
recipes.swap_it: No tomato? Grated carrot adds colour and a little sweetness instead.
recipes.closing_line: Bread having an identity crisis, in the best way.

recipes.title: Spiced Chana Roti Wrap
recipes.tagline: Leftover chana masala or plain boiled chickpeas, wrapped up for an easy, filling meal.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: If you’ve got leftover chana masala from another recipe in this book, this is the fastest, most satisfying way to give it a second life.
steps: If the chickpeas are cold from the fridge, warm them in a pan on medium heat for about 2 minutes, stirring occasionally, or microwave them for about 45 seconds.
Warm the roti too, either over a low flame for a few seconds per side, or in the same pan you used for the chickpeas.
Lay the warm roti flat on a plate. Spoon the warm chickpeas onto it, positioning them slightly toward one edge rather than dead centre.
Scatter the sliced onion over the chickpeas.
Cut a lemon in half and squeeze one half over the filling.
Fold the near edge of the roti over the filling first, then continue rolling the rest of the way, tucking in as you go so the filling stays contained.
recipes.money_hack: This is the perfect next-day use for leftover chana masala from the Chana Masala Rice Bowl recipe — no extra cooking required.
recipes.swap_it: No leftover chana masala? Plain boiled chickpeas with a pinch of chaat masala works as a simpler filling.
recipes.closing_line: Yesterday’s dinner, today’s lunch, zero extra effort.

recipes.title: Leftover Sabzi Roti Roll
recipes.tagline: The single best way to make sure last night’s vegetable curry doesn’t go to waste.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Mashing a wet sabzi slightly before rolling gives you a thicker filling that holds together properly — a runny filling is the main reason rolls fall apart.

ingredients.raw: ¾ cup leftover sabzi (any vegetable curry)
ingredients.name: leftover sabzi

steps: Warm the leftover sabzi in a pan on medium heat for about 2 minutes, stirring occasionally, or in the microwave for about 45 seconds — you want it properly hot, not just lukewarm.
Look at the sabzi. If it looks particularly wet or saucy, mash it lightly with a fork for a few seconds to bring it together into a slightly thicker mixture.
Warm the roti separately, either over a low flame or in a dry pan, until soft and bendable.
Lay the roti flat. Spoon the sabzi onto it, positioned toward one edge.
If using lemon, cut it in half and squeeze one half over the filling.
Roll the roti tightly starting from the edge closest to the filling, tucking in as you go, and eat immediately while everything is warm.
recipes.money_hack: This is exactly why it’s worth cooking a slightly bigger batch of any vegetable curry — today’s dinner becomes tomorrow’s easy lunch.
recipes.swap_it: No leftover sabzi? A quick mash of boiled potato with any spices you have makes a reasonable stand-in filling.
recipes.closing_line: This is what leftovers were always meant to become.

recipes.title: Boiled Egg Chaat
recipes.tagline: Boiled eggs, chopped up and tossed with a tangy, crunchy mix.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Chopping the boiled egg into rough, uneven pieces rather than neat slices helps it pick up seasoning far more effectively — the broken, textured surfaces catch the chaat masala and lemon.
steps: Place the eggs in a small pan and cover them with water. Put the pan on the stove and turn the flame to high.
Once the water is at a full, rolling boil (big bubbles everywhere), set a timer for 9 minutes.

When the timer ends, use a spoon to carefully lift the eggs out and drop them into a bowl of cold water. Leave them there for 2 minutes — this makes peeling much easier and stops the yolk from turning grey.

Peel each egg: tap it gently all over on a hard surface until the shell cracks in several places, then start peeling from the wider end, where there’s often a small air gap you can get your thumbnail under.
Place the peeled eggs on a cutting board. Using a knife, chop them into rough, uneven chunks — not neat cubes, just cut across a few times in different directions.
Put the chopped egg into a bowl. Add the finely chopped onion and tomato.
Sprinkle a pinch of chaat masala and a pinch of salt over the top.
Cut a lemon in half and squeeze one half over the bowl.
Toss everything together very gently with a spoon — egg yolk crumbles easily, so don’t stir hard. Top with coriander if using, and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Boil a batch of 4–5 eggs at once — extras keep in the fridge for a few days and turn any meal into a quick protein boost.
recipes.swap_it: No chaat masala? A mix of salt, a pinch of cumin powder, and black pepper works as a substitute.
recipes.closing_line: Simple, tangy, and gone faster than you’d expect.

recipes.title: Egg Bhurji Sandwich
recipes.tagline: Spiced scrambled egg, pressed between bread instead of rolled into a wrap.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cooking the bhurji a little drier than usual — with less visible moisture in the pan — is what stops the bread from turning soggy within minutes of assembling.
steps: Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook for about 2 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, and salt. Stir for a few seconds.
Crack both eggs into the pan. Wait 5 seconds, then start breaking the yolks and folding everything together with your spoon.

Keep cooking and folding for about 1 minute 30 seconds — a bit longer than you’d cook bhurji to eat on its own — until the mixture looks dry and crumbly rather than glossy and wet. Any extra moisture here will make the sandwich soggy later.
Turn off the stove and let the bhurji cool for about 1 minute before the next step — spreading hot filling straight onto bread creates steam that makes it damp almost instantly.
Lay out 2 slices of bread. Using a spoon, spread the bhurji generously and evenly across both, right to the edges.
Place the other 2 slices on top to close the sandwiches.

If toasting: butter the outside of both slices, place in a pan on medium heat, and press down gently with your spatula. Cook for about 1 minute per side, until golden. If skipping toasting, just cut and eat.
recipes.money_hack: This is a great way to turn one egg’s worth of bhurji into a filling meal by padding it out with extra bread.
recipes.swap_it: No onion? A pinch of any dried herb mixed into the eggs still gives good flavour.
recipes.closing_line: Handheld comfort food, no plate required.

recipes.title: Microwave Steamed Egg Bowl
recipes.tagline: Soft, custardy, savoury steamed egg — made entirely in the microwave.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Microwaving on reduced power cooks the egg far more gently than a hot pan — full power turns it rubbery and full of holes almost instantly, so the power level here matters more than anything else.

ingredients.raw: A few drops of soy sauce or a pinch of pepper (optional)
ingredients.name: few drops of soy sauce

steps: Crack both eggs into a microwave-safe bowl.
Add the water or milk and a pinch of salt.
Using a fork, beat everything together just until combined — don’t whisk in a lot of air bubbles, which causes uneven cooking with holes later.

Set your microwave to medium power — around 50–60% if your microwave has a power setting. This is the single most important step; skipping it and using full power will overcook parts of the egg before the rest even sets.
Microwave for 1 minute. Stop and open the door to check — the edges should look just barely set while the centre is still visibly liquid.
Close the door and microwave for another 30 seconds. Check again.

Keep repeating in 30-second bursts, checking each time, until the egg is mostly set but still looks a little wobbly and glossy in the very centre — it’s better to slightly undercook here, since it keeps firming up from residual heat once you take it out.
Let it rest for 1 minute without touching it.
Drizzle with soy sauce or a pinch of pepper, and eat straight from the bowl.
recipes.money_hack: Using milk instead of water gives a noticeably richer, smoother result for the same cost difference of a few rupees.
recipes.swap_it: No microwave-safe bowl? Any heatproof glass or ceramic bowl works, as long as it’s microwave-safe.
recipes.closing_line: Soft, gentle, and possibly the easiest hot meal in this entire book.

recipes.title: Egg Curry with Bread
recipes.tagline: The same comforting egg curry, served with bread instead of rice for a change.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Bread mops and scoops rather than absorbing the way rice does, so the gravy here is made a little thicker than usual so it clings to the bread instead of running off.
steps: If you haven’t already, boil the eggs: cover with water in a small pan, bring to a boil on high heat, boil for 9 minutes, then transfer to cold water for 2 minutes and peel.
Put a pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook for about 4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it turns deep golden-brown, not just soft.
Add the chopped tomato. Cook for 3–4 minutes, mashing gently with your spoon, until it fully breaks down into a soft, glossy mixture.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, garam masala, and salt. Stir for about 1 minute.
Add a small splash of water — noticeably less than you’d use if serving this over rice, since you want a thicker gravy this time that clings to bread rather than running off.
Let it simmer for 3–4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens slightly.
Using a knife, halve the boiled eggs lengthwise.
Nestle the egg halves into the gravy, cut-side up, and spoon a little sauce over the yolks. Warm through for about 1 minute without stirring vigorously.
Turn off the stove and serve with bread on the side, for mopping up the gravy.
recipes.money_hack: This is a good way to use bread that isn’t quite fresh enough for a sandwich but is perfectly fine for mopping up gravy.
recipes.swap_it: No bread? Rice or even plain roti works just as well alongside this curry.
recipes.closing_line: Different base, same comfort.

recipes.title: Egg Aloo Bhurji
recipes.tagline: Scrambled egg and mashed potato cooked together — twice the filling power.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Mashed potato added to bhurji makes it noticeably creamier and heartier than the egg-only version, and it barely takes any extra time.
steps: If your boiled potato is still hot, let it cool for a few minutes before mashing — a very hot potato releases steam that can make the final bhurji slightly gluey.
Put the potato in a bowl. Using a fork, mash it, leaving some small lumps rather than mashing it completely smooth — those lumps add texture to the finished dish.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook for about 2 minutes, until soft.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, and salt. Stir for a few seconds.
Add the mashed potato and mix it through, breaking it up as you stir so it combines evenly with the onion and spice rather than sitting in one dense clump.
Crack both eggs directly on top of the potato mixture.

Scramble everything together, folding continuously with your spoon, until the eggs are just cooked through and evenly mixed in — the whole thing should turn a uniform pale yellow, with no separate patches of plain potato and plain egg.
Turn off the stove and serve immediately.
recipes.money_hack: This recipe is a great way to use up a single leftover boiled potato that’s not quite enough for a full dish on its own.
recipes.swap_it: No potato on hand? Regular egg bhurji works fine without it — just skip that step.
recipes.closing_line: Two humble ingredients, one very filling result.

recipes.title: Light Egg Drop Soup
recipes.tagline: Warm, brothy, and the closest this book gets to a hug in a bowl.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Pouring the beaten egg in slowly while stirring gently is what creates soft, feathery ribbons — pour it in all at once and you get a few large, rubbery clumps instead.

ingredients.raw: ½ tsp cornflour (optional, for slight thickness) mixed with a little water
ingredients.name: cornflour

steps: Crack the egg into a small bowl or cup and beat it with a fork until smooth. Set aside.
Pour the water into a pan, put it on the stove, and turn the flame to medium-high. Bring it to a gentle boil, about 2–3 minutes.
Season with a pinch of salt and pepper.

If using cornflour: in a small cup, mix the cornflour with 1 tablespoon of cold water until fully dissolved with no lumps. Pour this into the simmering broth and stir. Let it simmer for 1 minute until it thickens very slightly and turns a bit glossy.
Turn the flame down to low, so the broth is at a gentle simmer, not a hard boil — a rolling boil will turn the egg into tough clumps almost instantly.

Hold the beaten egg a few inches above the pan. With one hand, drizzle it in very slowly in a thin, steady stream. At the same time, with your other hand, stir the broth gently in one consistent circular direction.
Keep this up for about 10–15 seconds until all the egg is in.
Turn off the stove the moment the egg looks just set — it happens fast, usually within seconds of finishing the pour.
Top with spring onion or coriander if using, and serve immediately.
recipes.money_hack: This is an excellent way to use a single egg when you don’t have enough for a full omelette or bhurji.
recipes.swap_it: No cornflour? Skip it — the soup will be thinner, but just as comforting.
recipes.closing_line: This is what a bad day deserves to end with.

recipes.title: Spiced Curd Egg Mash
recipes.tagline: A cooling, protein-packed mash that works as a spread, a dip, or a meal on its own.
recipes.equipment_text: Kettle or one pan (to boil eggs)
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Mashing boiled egg into curd rather than mayonnaise gives you something lighter and tangier, closer to a raita than an egg salad.
steps: Boil and peel the eggs the usual way: cover with water, boil for 9 minutes, cool in cold water for 2 minutes, then peel.
Let the eggs sit for another minute or two so they’re not too hot to handle comfortably.

Place the eggs in a bowl. Using a fork, mash them roughly — press down and turn the fork to break them up, leaving a coarse, uneven texture with visible bits of yolk and white, not a completely smooth paste.
Add the curd and mix thoroughly, folding it through the mashed egg with a spoon until evenly combined.
Sprinkle in a pinch of chaat masala, a pinch of pepper, and a pinch of salt.
Mix again, then taste a small spoonful — curd varies in tanginess, so adjust the seasoning if needed.
Top with coriander if using, and serve with bread, roti, or crackers, or eat straight with a spoon.
recipes.money_hack: This is a great way to use eggs that were boiled a day or two ago and are sitting in the fridge waiting for a purpose.
recipes.swap_it: No curd? Mashed avocado or a little mayonnaise works if you have either, though the flavour will be quite different.
recipes.closing_line: Cool, tangy, and quietly one of the more versatile things in this book.

recipes.title: Butter Masala Fried Egg
recipes.tagline: A sunny-side-up egg, dressed up with butter and a proper spice mix.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Sprinkling the spices on while the egg is still cooking, rather than after, lets them partially cook into the surface instead of just sitting loose on top.
steps: Put your pan on the stove, add the butter, and turn the flame to medium.
Wait for the butter to fully melt and just start to foam slightly at the edges — this takes about 30–45 seconds and is a good sign the pan is at the right temperature.
Crack the first egg gently into the pan, trying to keep the yolk whole and centred. Crack the second egg in beside it, leaving a little space so the whites don’t run into each other too much.

While the whites are still mostly see-through and just starting to turn opaque at the edges (this happens quickly, within about 20 seconds), sprinkle the chilli powder, chaat masala, and salt evenly over the top.

Let the eggs cook without touching them. Watch the whites — you’re waiting for them to turn fully opaque and set all the way through, while the yolk still looks glossy and slightly soft when you gently shake the pan. This takes about 2–3 minutes.
If you prefer a firmer yolk, let it cook 1 more minute, checking every 20 seconds since it can go from soft to fully hard quite quickly at this stage.
Turn off the stove and slide the eggs out onto a plate.
recipes.money_hack: Butter makes a noticeable difference here over oil, but a mix of half butter, half oil stretches your butter further without losing much flavour.
recipes.swap_it: No chaat masala? A simple mix of salt and black pepper still makes a great fried egg.
recipes.closing_line: Same egg you’ve always made, dressed up like it means something.

recipes.title: Egg and Spinach Scramble
recipes.tagline: A quick way to sneak some greens into an otherwise simple egg dish.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Spinach releases a lot of water as it cooks, which is why it needs to fully wilt down before the eggs go in — otherwise that moisture leaks into the eggs and leaves you with a watery scramble.
steps: Wash the spinach leaves under running water, then roughly chop them on a cutting board.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook for about 2 minutes, until soft.
Add the chopped spinach — it will look like a lot at first, filling the pan right up, but don’t worry, it shrinks dramatically as it cooks.
Stir frequently for about 2 minutes, until it’s fully wilted down to roughly a quarter of its original size, with no dry leaves left standing.
Look at the pan — if there’s a noticeable pool of liquid, let it cook for another 30 seconds to reduce slightly.
Crack both eggs directly on top of the wilted spinach. Add a pinch of salt and pepper.

Scramble everything together with a folding motion, cooking until the eggs are just set and no longer glossy — the spinach should be spread evenly through as green flecks, not sitting in a separate layer.
Turn off the stove and serve immediately.
recipes.money_hack: Spinach is one of the cheaper leafy greens available seasonally — buy a bunch and use half here, half in another recipe within a day or two.
recipes.swap_it: No spinach? Any other leafy green you have access to works with the same method.
recipes.closing_line: Green, filling, and still ready in ten minutes.

recipes.title: Egg-Coated Paratha (Anda Paratha)
recipes.tagline: A plain paratha or roti, dipped in beaten egg and pan-fried until golden.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Pressing the roti into the beaten egg and holding it there for a moment lets the surface actually soak up a thin layer, so the egg cooks into a genuine golden crust instead of sliding off.

ingredients.raw: 1 roti or plain paratha (leftover or freshly made)
ingredients.name: roti

steps: Crack the egg into a shallow bowl or plate — wide enough that the roti can lie flat in it.
Add a pinch of salt, pepper, and chilli flakes. Beat with a fork until smooth.
Lay the roti into the beaten egg. Press down gently with your fingers and hold for a few seconds so the surface soaks up some of the egg, rather than the egg just sitting on top.
Flip the roti over in the egg and repeat on the other side.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds until it looks hot and shimmery.
Carefully place the egg-coated roti into the pan.
Don’t move it for the first minute — this undisturbed time is what lets a proper golden crust form instead of a patchy, torn one.
After about 2 minutes, check underneath with your spatula — it should look set and golden at the edges. Flip carefully.
Cook the second side for another 2 minutes, until evenly golden and the egg is fully cooked through with no runny patches visible at the edges.
Slide it onto a plate, cut into strips if you like, and serve.
recipes.money_hack: This is an excellent way to turn a single leftover roti into a much more substantial, protein-rich meal.
recipes.swap_it: No leftover roti? Bread works with the same method, though the texture will be a little different.
recipes.closing_line: A leftover roti’s glow-up moment.

recipes.title: Paneer Bhurji
recipes.tagline: Paneer’s answer to egg bhurji — scrambled, spiced, and just as fast.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Paneer doesn’t scramble the way eggs do — it just crumbles and soaks up whatever it’s cooked in, so giving it enough time in the pan with the spices is what makes it taste properly seasoned rather than bland.
steps: Take the paneer block in your hands over a plate or the pan itself. Break it apart with your fingers into small, irregular crumbles — no need for a knife, this is actually faster and gives a better texture than cutting.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion and chilli, if using.
Cook for about 2 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion turns soft and just see-through at the edges.
Add the chopped tomato. Cook for about 2 minutes, mashing gently with your spoon, until it softens and turns a little saucy.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, and salt. Stir for a few seconds.
Add the crumbled paneer. Mix it through thoroughly so it’s coated in the onion-tomato mixture.
Let it cook for 2–3 minutes, stirring occasionally — this resting time in the pan is what lets the paneer properly soak up the flavour instead of just sitting there coated on the outside.
Turn off the stove and serve hot.
recipes.money_hack: Crumble the paneer with your hands rather than a knife — it creates a more authentic bhurji texture and saves you dirtying a cutting board.
recipes.swap_it: No paneer? Crumbled tofu (if available) works with a similar method and texture.
recipes.closing_line: Same comfort as egg bhurji, completely vegetarian.

recipes.title: Aloo Matar with Roti
recipes.tagline: Potato and peas in a simple, spiced gravy — an absolute classic for good reason.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A properly browned onion and a fully broken-down tomato are what give a simple curry its depth — rushing through those two steps is the most common reason a home version tastes thinner than you remember.
steps: If your potatoes aren’t boiled yet, put them whole in a pot of water, bring to a boil, and cook for about 15–20 minutes until a knife slides in easily. Drain, cool slightly, peel, and cut into cubes.
Put a pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the chopped onion.
Cook, stirring occasionally, for about 4 minutes — you want a proper golden-brown colour here, not just soft, so be patient.

Add the chopped tomato. Cook for 3–4 minutes, mashing it gently against the pan with your spoon, until it completely collapses into a soft, jammy texture — you’ll see a little oil separate at the edges when it’s ready.
Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, garam masala, and salt. Stir for about 1 minute.
Add the boiled potato cubes and the peas, along with a splash of water — enough to loosen everything into a gravy, not a dry sauté.

Let it simmer for 5–8 minutes, stirring occasionally. Partway through, press a potato cube or two gently against the pan with your spoon — this releases a little starch and thickens the gravy naturally.
The peas are done once they’re tender but still bright green, not dull and overcooked. Turn off the stove and serve hot with roti.
recipes.money_hack: Boiling potatoes in bulk once and using them across several recipes during the week saves both time and gas or electricity.
recipes.swap_it: No fresh peas? Frozen peas work identically and don’t need any extra prep.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Potatoes — ₹6, Peas — ₹6, Vegetables/spices — ₹5, Roti — ₹5. Estimated total — ₹22.
recipes.closing_line: This is the dish that makes a rented room feel a little more like home.

recipes.title: Simple Palak Dal
recipes.tagline: Spinach cooked into dal — an easy way to get greens into a meal you were already going to make.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Adding the spinach only in the last few minutes keeps it bright green and fresh-tasting — add it too early and it turns dull and overcooked.

ingredients.raw: ¼ cup toor or moong dal
ingredients.name: toor

steps: Rinse the dal in a bowl: fill with water, swirl, pour off the cloudy water while holding the dal back, repeat once or twice.
Put the rinsed dal into a pot, add the 2 cups of water and a pinch of turmeric.
Put the pot on the stove and turn the flame to high. Bring it to a boil, about 3 minutes.
Turn the flame down to a simmer. Cook for about 12 minutes, mashing gently with the back of your spoon every few minutes, until it breaks down into a thick, soupy consistency.
While the dal simmers, wash and roughly chop the spinach on a cutting board.
In the last 3–4 minutes of the dal’s cooking time, stir the chopped spinach directly into the pot and let it wilt in the hot dal — don’t add it any earlier than this.
While that finishes, make the tempering: heat the oil in a small separate pan on medium heat, add the cumin seeds, and wait about 10 seconds for them to sizzle.
Add the chopped onion to the tempering pan and cook for about 2 minutes until golden.
Pour the hot tempering directly into the pot of dal — it will sizzle loudly on contact, which is exactly right.
Add salt to taste, stir once, and serve with rice or roti.
recipes.money_hack: This is a good way to use spinach that’s starting to wilt — it’s going into a simmering dal anyway, so texture matters less.
recipes.swap_it: No spinach? Any other leafy green, or even grated bottle gourd, works with the same method.
recipes.closing_line: Greens, protein, and comfort, all in one pot.

recipes.title: Mild Coconut Vegetable Stew
recipes.tagline: A gentle, lightly sweet stew inspired by South Indian coconut-based curries.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Coconut milk can split or turn grainy if boiled too hard, so keeping the heat gentle once it goes in is what gives you that smooth, comforting texture.

ingredients.raw: 1 cup mixed vegetables (potato, carrot, beans, peas — whatever you have)
ingredients.name: mixed vegetables

ingredients.raw: ½ cup coconut milk (or 2 tbsp desiccated coconut blended with ½ cup water)
ingredients.name: coconut milk

steps: On a cutting board, chop the vegetables you’re using into roughly bite-sized, similar-sized pieces.
Put a pot on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium.
If using curry leaves, add them now and let them crackle for a few seconds.
Add the chopped onion. Cook for about 2 minutes, until soft.
Add the mixed vegetables and cook for 2 minutes, stirring to coat them lightly in the oil.
Pour in the coconut milk, adding a splash of water too if the mixture looks thick.
Turn the flame down to low, so it’s at a very gentle simmer — small, slow bubbles, not a rolling boil, since coconut milk can separate under too much heat.
Cook uncovered for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, keeping the heat low the entire time.
Check doneness by piercing the largest piece of vegetable (usually potato or carrot) with a fork — it should slide in easily with no resistance.
Season with pepper and salt, tasting a small spoonful before adding more, since coconut milk’s natural sweetness affects how much salt you’ll want. Turn off the stove and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Small tetra packs of coconut milk are more economical than buying a fresh coconut for one recipe, and they keep in the fridge for a few days once opened.
recipes.swap_it: No coconut milk at all? A splash of milk with a pinch of sugar approximates some of the richness, though the flavour will be different.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Vegetables — ₹10, Coconut milk — ₹12, Spices/oil — ₹4. Estimated total — ₹26.
recipes.closing_line: Gentle, mild, and a nice break from the usual spice level.

recipes.title: Smoky Mashed Eggplant (Baingan Bharta Shortcut)
recipes.tagline: A stovetop shortcut for the classic smoky roasted eggplant mash.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Covering the pan while the eggplant cooks traps steam that softens it much faster than cooking it uncovered — you won’t get quite the same smokiness as an open-flame roast, but the texture gets close.
steps: Wash the eggplant and cut it into rough chunks on a cutting board, about the size of large dice.
Put a pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium-low. Add the eggplant chunks.
Cover immediately with a lid — the trapped steam softens the eggplant much faster than leaving it uncovered.

Cook for 10–12 minutes, stirring every few minutes (put the lid back on each time after stirring). You’re waiting for the eggplant to become completely soft and almost fall apart when pressed with your spoon.
Once soft, mash it roughly right in the pan using the back of your spoon, leaving some texture rather than mashing it into a completely smooth purée.
Push the mashed eggplant to one side of the pan. Add a touch more oil if the pan looks dry, and add the chopped onion to the empty space.
Cook the onion for about 2 minutes, until soft, then add the tomato and cook for 2–3 minutes until it breaks down.
Mix the mashed eggplant back into the onion-tomato base. Add a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, and salt.
Cook for 3–4 more minutes, stirring occasionally, until everything is well combined and heated through.
Turn off the stove, top with coriander if using, and serve.
recipes.money_hack: Eggplant is often one of the cheaper seasonal vegetables — buy it when it’s in season for the best price.
recipes.swap_it: No eggplant? Mashed, roasted or boiled potato with the same onion-tomato base makes a different but still tasty dish.
recipes.closing_line: Smoky, soft, and a lot more impressive than the ten-minute prep suggests.

recipes.title: Besan Curd Kadhi
recipes.tagline: A tangy, warming besan-and-curd curry, best eaten with rice.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Kadhi splits or turns lumpy when the curd and besan aren’t whisked completely smooth before any heat is involved — getting that step right first avoids the problem entirely.
steps: Put the curd and besan together in a bowl — no water yet. Whisk them together thoroughly with a fork or whisk until completely smooth, with no lumps of besan anywhere. This is much easier to do now than after water’s been added.
Gradually whisk in the water, a little at a time, along with a pinch of turmeric and salt, until you have a completely smooth, thin mixture.
Pour this into a pot and place it on the stove on medium heat.
Stir frequently and continuously as it heats up — this constant stirring in the early stages is what prevents the curd from splitting.
Once it reaches a gentle boil (small bubbles across the surface), turn the flame down to low.
Let it simmer for 10–12 minutes, stirring every minute or so, until it thickens slightly to a consistency similar to a thin gravy.
While it simmers, make the tempering: heat the oil in a small separate pan on medium heat, add the mustard and cumin seeds, and let them pop for about 10 seconds.
Pour this tempering over the finished kadhi just before serving, and serve with rice.
recipes.money_hack: Slightly sour curd (a day or two past its best) actually works better in kadhi than very fresh curd — it gives a proper tang.
recipes.swap_it: No mustard seeds for the tempering? Just cumin seeds in the oil still gives good flavour.
recipes.closing_line: Tangy, warm, and a nice change of pace from the usual curries.

recipes.title: Everyday Mixed Vegetable Sabzi
recipes.tagline: A simple, dry-style vegetable curry that goes with anything — rice, roti, or even bread.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cutting all the vegetables to a similar size is what matters most here — evenly sized pieces cook at the same rate, so you don’t end up with raw potato next to mushy cauliflower.

ingredients.raw: 1.5 cups mixed vegetables (potato, beans, carrot, cauliflower — whatever’s available)
ingredients.name: mixed vegetables

steps: On a cutting board, chop all your vegetables into roughly the same size pieces, about bite-sized — this matters more than which specific vegetables you use.
Put a pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Add the cumin seeds.
Wait about 10 seconds for them to sizzle, then add the chopped onion.
Cook for about 2 minutes, until soft.
Add all the mixed vegetables, a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, and salt. Stir well so everything gets an even coating of spice.
Cover with a lid and turn the flame down to low-medium.
Cook for 12–15 minutes, stirring every 3–4 minutes (putting the lid back on each time) to check on progress and prevent sticking.
If it looks like it’s starting to catch on the bottom of the pan, add a small splash of water.
Test doneness by pushing a fork into the largest, hardest piece — usually potato or carrot. It’s done once the fork slides in with no resistance.
Turn off the stove and serve.
recipes.money_hack: This is the perfect recipe for using up small amounts of several different vegetables that aren’t enough on their own for a full dish.
recipes.swap_it: No specific vegetables? Literally any combination works — this recipe is built around flexibility, not a fixed ingredient list.
recipes.closing_line: Not exciting. Just reliably, quietly good.

recipes.title: Simple Stuffed Capsicum
recipes.tagline: Bell peppers filled with spiced mashed potato — looks impressive, isn’t hard at all.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Cooking the stuffed capsicum cut-side up, covered, lets it steam gently from the inside while the bottom slowly chars against the pan — a properly cooked pepper without needing an oven at all.
steps: Wash the capsicums. Using a knife, cut each one in half through the stem, top to bottom.
Using a spoon, carefully scoop out the seeds and white membrane from inside each half, trying not to tear the flesh — a torn capsicum won’t hold its filling well.
Put the mashed potato in a bowl. Add the chopped onion, a pinch of turmeric, chilli powder, garam masala, and salt. Mix thoroughly with a spoon until evenly combined.

Spoon this mixture into each capsicum half, pressing it down gently with the back of your spoon so it’s compact and doesn’t have large air gaps. Mound it slightly above the rim if you have extra filling.
Put a pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to low-medium.
Arrange the stuffed capsicums in the pan, cut-side facing up.
Cover immediately with a lid — the trapped steam is what cooks the capsicum through without needing to flip it, which would spill the filling.
Cook for 12–15 minutes without lifting the lid too often.
Check doneness by gently pressing a capsicum with a fork — it should yield easily rather than feeling firm and raw. If you peek underneath one, you should see light charring on the base.
Turn off the stove and serve.
recipes.money_hack: This is a great way to use up potatoes you’ve already boiled for another recipe — no extra cooking step needed for the filling base.
recipes.swap_it: No capsicum? The same spiced potato filling works well wrapped in a roti instead.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Capsicum — ₹10, Potatoes — ₹6, Onion/spices — ₹5, Oil — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹23.
recipes.closing_line: Looks like you tried much harder than you did. Keep that between us.

recipes.title: Spiced Roasted Makhana
recipes.tagline: Fox nuts, roasted with a bit of spice, until they turn into an oddly addictive crunchy snack.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Low, steady heat slowly drives the moisture out of makhana until it turns light and crackly — rushing this with high heat just browns the outside while the inside stays soft.
steps: Put your pan on the stove, add the ghee, and turn the flame to low-medium — resist turning it up higher, since makhana needs gentle, even heat to crisp all the way through.
Wait about 20 seconds for the ghee to melt.
Add the makhana, spreading it out in as close to a single layer as your pan allows.
Stir frequently — every 20–30 seconds — for 5–6 minutes.

To test if it’s done: take one piece out, let it cool for a few seconds, then tap it against the side of the pan or bite it gently. It should sound and feel hollow and light, and crisp when you bite it — not soft or chewy. If it still feels chewy, keep roasting in 1-minute bursts, testing each time.
Once properly crisp, turn off the stove. While the makhana is still warm, sprinkle over the chilli powder, chaat masala, and salt.
Toss immediately so the residual heat and light oiliness help the spices stick to every piece.
recipes.money_hack: Makhana can be pricier per packet than other snacks, but a single cup goes a long way and keeps well in an airtight container for future late nights.
recipes.swap_it: No chaat masala? Plain salt and pepper still makes a satisfying version.
recipes.closing_line: Crunchy enough to make you forget you’re supposed to be sleeping.

recipes.title: Stovetop Masala Popcorn
recipes.tagline: No microwave popcorn packets needed — just a pan, some kernels, and a bit of patience.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Managing the heat evenly is the whole technique here — too low and the kernels won’t build enough pressure to pop; too high and you’ll scorch the ones that have already popped.
steps: Put your pan (one with a lid) on the stove, add the oil, and turn the flame to medium.
Add just 2 or 3 kernels first and wait, with the lid off, watching them — when they pop, that’s your sign the oil and pan are at the right temperature.
Add the rest of the kernels in as close to a single layer as you can, then immediately cover with the lid.

Every 15–20 seconds, pick up the pan by the handle and shake it gently side to side over the heat, without lifting the lid — this helps unpopped kernels get even contact with the hot surface and stops popped ones from burning.

Listen closely to the popping sound. Once it slows down from rapid, constant popping to a gap of 2–3 seconds between pops, remove the pan from the heat right away — don’t wait for complete silence, or you risk scorching the last few kernels.
Take the lid off carefully (steam will escape) and pour the popcorn into a bowl.
While it’s still warm, sprinkle with salt and your chosen spice, and toss well so the seasoning sticks to the slightly oily surface.
