recipes.money_hack: A bag of loose popcorn kernels is far cheaper per serving than any packaged or microwave popcorn — and lasts for many, many late nights.
recipes.swap_it: No specific seasoning? Even plain salted popcorn is a perfectly good late-night snack.
recipes.closing_line: Cheaper than a movie ticket snack, and you don’t even have to leave your room.

recipes.title: Jhaal Muri (Spiced Puffed Rice)
recipes.tagline: A Kolkata street-food classic — puffed rice tossed with a punchy, tangy mix.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Puffed rice is extremely absorbent, so this needs to be tossed and eaten right away — left sitting even ten minutes, it soaks up moisture from the vegetables and turns soft.

ingredients.raw: 1 tsp mustard oil (or any oil) and a squeeze of lemon
ingredients.name: mustard oil

steps: Before touching the puffed rice, get everything else ready first: finely chop the onion, tomato, and chilli, and have your peanuts, masala, oil, and a cut lemon within reach.
Put the puffed rice into a large bowl — choose one with enough room that you can toss without it spilling over the sides.
Add the chopped onion, tomato, chilli, and peanuts.
Sprinkle a pinch of chaat masala and a pinch of salt evenly over the top.
Drizzle the mustard oil over everything.
Squeeze the lemon over the bowl too.
Toss immediately and thoroughly, lifting the mixture from the bottom and turning it over rather than stirring flat, so the dressing reaches every piece.
Eat right away — this is a “make it and eat it in the same minute” recipe, since the crisp texture is the entire point.
recipes.money_hack: Puffed rice is sold very cheaply in bulk — it’s one of the most cost-effective snack bases available anywhere in India.
recipes.swap_it: No mustard oil? Regular oil with an extra squeeze of lemon gets you close to the same sharp flavour.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Puffed rice — ₹6, Vegetables/peanuts — ₹5, Masala/oil — ₹3. Estimated total — ₹14.
recipes.closing_line: Loud, tangy, crunchy — exactly what late-night hunger is asking for.

recipes.title: Dry Roasted Masala Chickpeas
recipes.tagline: A crunchy, spiced snack made from chickpeas you’ve already boiled.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Drying the chickpeas thoroughly before they hit the pan is the single biggest factor in whether they crisp or stay soft — any leftover surface moisture just steams them instead of roasting them.
steps: Drain the chickpeas thoroughly in a sieve.

Spread them out on a clean kitchen towel or a few sheets of paper towel. Pat them dry, gently rolling and pressing so the towel absorbs moisture from all sides — don’t skip this, it’s what determines whether you get crisp chickpeas or steamed ones.
Put your pan on the stove, add 1 teaspoon of oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds until it looks hot and shimmery.
Add the dried chickpeas.
Roast, stirring frequently so they cook evenly on all sides rather than just the bottom, for 6–8 minutes.
Watch for the colour to deepen slightly and small cracks or blisters to appear on some of the skins — both are signs they’re crisping properly.
Turn off the stove. While still hot, sprinkle with chilli powder, chaat masala, and salt.
Toss immediately so the seasoning sticks to the warm, slightly oily surface.
recipes.money_hack: Making sure the chickpeas are well drained and dry before roasting helps them crisp up properly instead of steaming in the pan.
recipes.swap_it: No boiled chickpeas ready? Canned chickpeas, drained and dried with a paper towel, work just as well.
recipes.closing_line: A snack that’s actually doing you a favour, for once.

recipes.title: Quick Onion Pakora
recipes.tagline: Crispy, spiced onion fritters — the ultimate rainy-evening snack.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Salted onion releases its own water, which is what binds this batter together — trust that process instead of pouring in extra water too early, or the mixture gets too wet to shape.
steps: Peel the onion and slice it thinly on a cutting board.
Put the sliced onion in a bowl. Add the besan, chilli powder, carom seeds, and a pinch of salt.
Mix everything together with your hands for about 30 seconds — you’re working the salt into the onion, which starts drawing out moisture.
Let the mixture sit for 1–2 minutes. You’ll notice it becoming slightly wetter and clumpier on its own as the onion releases water.
Check the texture: if it’s still too dry and crumbly to hold together when you squeeze a bit in your hand, add just a small splash of water — not a lot, add a teaspoon at a time.
Put your pan on the stove, add the oil, and turn the flame to medium. Wait 30 seconds for it to heat.
Using a spoon, scoop up a small portion of the mixture and drop it into the pan, then flatten it slightly with the back of the spoon so it cooks through evenly rather than staying raw in the centre.
Repeat with the rest of the mixture, leaving space between each one.
Fry for about 3 minutes, then check the underside by lifting one edge with your spatula — you want a deep golden-brown colour with visibly crisp edges before flipping.
Flip each one and fry the second side for another 3 minutes, checking the same way. Remove and serve hot.
recipes.money_hack: Shallow-frying in a pan instead of deep-frying uses far less oil while still getting a good crisp texture.
recipes.swap_it: No carom seeds? Cumin seeds work as a substitute, though the flavour will be slightly different.
recipes.closing_line: Rain outside, crispy pakoras inside — perfect trade.

recipes.title: Midnight Cheese Toast Melt
recipes.tagline: For the exam-night hunger that specifically wants something warm, cheesy, and immediate.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Low heat and a little patience lets the cheese melt through fully by the time the bread turns golden — high heat browns the outside long before the inside has warmed at all.

ingredients.raw: 1 cheese slice (or a small handful of grated cheese)
ingredients.name: cheese slice

ingredients.raw: Pinch of chilli flakes or oregano
ingredients.name: chilli flakes

steps: Using a butter knife, spread butter on one side of each bread slice, covering right to the edges.
Place the cheese slice between the two pieces of bread, with the buttered sides facing outward on both.
Put a dry pan on the stove and turn the flame to low-medium — genuinely lower than feels natural, since this needs time for the heat to reach the cheese in the middle.
Place the sandwich into the pan.
Press down gently and evenly with your spatula for a few seconds — this good contact helps the heat transfer through faster.
Let it cook for about 2 minutes. Check the underside by lifting an edge — you want a deep, even golden-brown, which usually means the cheese inside is at least halfway melted.
Flip the sandwich over and press down again with your spatula.
Cook the second side for another 2 minutes, until equally golden.
Remove from the pan, sprinkle with chilli flakes or oregano, and cut in half. Let it cool for about 30 seconds before biting — the cheese inside will be very hot.
recipes.money_hack: Keep a few cheese slices in the fridge specifically for nights like this — they last for weeks and are worth the small investment for exam season alone.
recipes.swap_it: No cheese? A thick layer of butter and a sprinkle of chaat masala makes a different but still comforting version.
recipes.closing_line: Studying can wait four minutes. Eat this first.

recipes.title: Crispy Masala Papad Nachos
recipes.tagline: Broken roasted papad, topped like nachos — crunchy, spicy, oddly satisfying.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A properly roasted papad puffs and crisps evenly and shatters cleanly when you bite it — exactly the textural contrast you want against the soft onion and tomato on top.
steps: If roasting over an open flame: hold the papad with tongs about an inch above the flame. Keep it moving constantly, turning and rotating it so every part gets even exposure. This takes about 10–15 seconds total — you’re watching for it to puff up slightly and darken evenly.

If using a dry pan instead: put it on medium heat, place the papad in, and press down firmly and evenly with a spatula, flipping every few seconds so it doesn’t scorch in one spot before the rest crisps.
Once evenly roasted (it should snap cleanly when you bend it, not bend softly), break it into large, irregular pieces with your hands and arrange them on a plate.
Scatter the chopped onion and tomato over the top, spreading it evenly so every piece of papad gets some topping.
Sprinkle with chaat masala.
Cut a lemon in half and squeeze one half over everything.
If using curd, add a small dollop now, positioned so it doesn’t touch every piece at once and make everything soggy immediately.
Serve right away, while the papad is still crisp.
recipes.money_hack: Papads are one of the cheapest crunchy snacks available and store for months unopened — always worth keeping a packet around.
recipes.swap_it: No curd? Skip it — the papad and toppings are still satisfying without it.
recipes.closing_line: Nacho night, minus the nachos, minus most of the cost.

recipes.title: Banana Chips Masala Chaat
recipes.tagline: Store-bought banana chips, given a quick chaat-style upgrade.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Squeezing the lemon on right before eating, not any earlier, is what keeps the chips crunchy — the acidity starts softening them almost immediately once it touches them.
steps: Put the banana chips into a bowl, choosing one with enough room to toss them gently without crushing too many.
Finely chop the onion on a cutting board and add it to the bowl.
Sprinkle a pinch of chaat masala and a pinch of chilli powder over the top.
Cut the lemon in half. Right before you’re ready to eat — not any earlier — squeeze one half over the bowl.
Toss gently and quickly, using a folding motion so the seasoning spreads without breaking too many chips.
Eat immediately, while the crunch is still at its best.
recipes.money_hack: Buy banana chips loose from a local shop rather than a branded packet — usually a better price for the same amount.
recipes.swap_it: No onion? The chaat masala and lemon alone still transform plain banana chips into something more interesting.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Banana chips — ₹12, Onion/masala — ₹3, Lemon — ₹1. Estimated total — ₹15.
recipes.closing_line: A packet snack that now tastes like you put in some effort.

recipes.title: Bread Halwa
recipes.tagline: A quick, sweet pudding made from bread, milk, and sugar — dessert with almost no shopping list.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Toasting the bread briefly in ghee before the milk goes in firms up the surface just enough that it absorbs the milk gradually, instead of instantly turning to mush.
steps: Tear the bread slices into small pieces with your hands.
Put your pan on the stove, add the ghee, and turn the flame to medium. Wait about 20 seconds for it to melt.
Add the torn bread pieces. Toss and stir for about 2 minutes, until they turn a shade golden and feel slightly firmer when you press one with your spoon.
Add the milk and sugar. Stir well to combine.
Turn the flame down to medium-low. Cook, stirring frequently — about every 30 seconds — for 5–6 minutes.

Watch the texture: the bread will gradually soften and swell as it absorbs the milk, and the mixture will thicken from loose and liquid to something that holds together when you drag your spoon through it.
Once thick and most of the milk is absorbed, stir in the cardamom powder. Cook for 30 more seconds.
Turn off the stove. Top with chopped nuts if using, and serve warm.
recipes.money_hack: This is an excellent way to use bread that’s a little stale — it soaks up the milk better than fresh bread.
recipes.swap_it: No milk? Water with an extra spoon of sugar works, though it won’t be as rich or creamy.
recipes.closing_line: Warm, sweet, and ready before you’ve even decided you deserve dessert.

recipes.title: Simple Suji Halwa
recipes.tagline: The classic semolina halwa — soft, ghee-rich, and endlessly comforting.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Roasting the semolina thoroughly before any liquid touches it is what gives the finished halwa its nutty depth of flavour, instead of tasting like plain sweetened porridge.
steps: Put your pan on the stove, add the ghee, and turn the flame to medium-low.
Once the ghee has melted (about 20 seconds), add the sooji.
Stir constantly and continuously — don’t walk away, since sooji can go from perfectly roasted to burnt within seconds if left unattended.
Keep stirring for 4–5 minutes, until the sooji turns a light golden colour and smells noticeably toasty and nutty, rather than raw and starchy.

While the sooji roasts, heat the water and sugar together in a separate small pan or kettle until the sugar fully dissolves — having this ready means you’re not scrambling to boil water the moment the sooji finishes.

With your sooji pan still on low heat, pour the hot sugar-water in very slowly, stirring vigorously and continuously as you pour — it will bubble and spit on contact, so pour from a slight distance and keep stirring the whole time to prevent lumps.

Once all the liquid is in, keep stirring over low heat for 2–3 minutes. Watch for the mixture to thicken and start pulling away from the sides of the pan slightly — that pulling-away is your clearest sign it’s ready.
Stir in the cardamom and nuts or raisins if using.
Turn off the stove and serve warm.
recipes.money_hack: Sooji and sugar are both cheap pantry staples — this dessert costs very little for how satisfying and generous a portion it makes.
recipes.swap_it: No cardamom? A drop of vanilla essence, if you have it, gives a different but pleasant flavour.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Sooji — ₹5, Sugar — ₹4, Ghee — ₹6, Nuts (optional) — ₹1. Estimated total — ₹16.
recipes.closing_line: This is what ”everything’s going to be fine” tastes like.

recipes.title: Microwave Chocolate Banana Mug Cake
recipes.tagline: A genuine mug cake, made in the microwave, with no oven and minimal cleanup.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Microwave cakes cook from the outside in, quite differently from oven-baked cakes, which is why checking early rather than assuming the full time is needed matters so much here.

ingredients.raw: 1 tbsp cocoa powder (if available) or 1 extra tbsp sugar
ingredients.name: cocoa powder

ingredients.raw: A tiny pinch of baking soda (optional, for a softer texture)
ingredients.name: tiny pinch of baking soda

steps: Peel the banana and put it directly into a large mug.
Using a fork, mash it against the side of the mug until mostly smooth, with just a few small lumps left.
Add the flour, cocoa powder (if using), sugar, milk, and baking soda (if using) into the same mug.
Stir with the fork just until you can’t see any dry flour anymore — about 15–20 stirs. Stop as soon as it looks combined; overmixing makes the finished cake denser.
Place the mug in the microwave. Set it to high power and microwave for 90 seconds.
Stop and check — don’t assume it needs longer without looking. Insert a knife or fork into the centre and pull it out.

If it comes out mostly clean, with maybe a few moist crumbs but no wet batter, it’s done. If it’s still wet, microwave in 15-second bursts, checking each time — mug cakes go from underdone to overcooked very quickly.
Let it cool for 1 minute before eating directly from the mug — it keeps cooking slightly from residual heat even after you take it out.
recipes.money_hack: No cocoa powder? Skip it entirely rather than buying it just for this — a plain banana mug cake is still genuinely good.
recipes.swap_it: No baking soda? The cake will be slightly denser, but still perfectly enjoyable.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Banana — ₹6, Flour/sugar — ₹5, Cocoa (optional) — ₹5, Milk — ₹2. Estimated total — ₹13 (₹18 with cocoa).
recipes.closing_line: A genuine treat, ready faster than you could’ve ordered dessert.

recipes.title: Sweet Lassi
recipes.tagline: A thick, cold, sweetened yoghurt drink — refreshing and filling at the same time.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: A proper minute of brisk whisking is what introduces air and fully breaks down the curd, giving you that classic thick, slightly frothy texture — a half-hearted stir leaves it thin and watery.

ingredients.raw: ¼ cup cold water or milk
ingredients.name: cold water

steps: Put the curd into a bowl or large glass first, before adding anything else.
Using a fork or small whisk, whisk it vigorously for about 30 seconds — moving fast, breaking up any lumps completely, until the curd looks smooth and slightly glossy.

Add the cold water or milk gradually, a little at a time, continuing to whisk briskly after each addition — this is what introduces the light frothiness lassi is known for, rather than just diluting the curd into a flat liquid.
Add the sugar and cardamom, if using.
Whisk once more, for about 15 seconds, until the sugar is fully dissolved — no gritty texture left.
Taste a small sip and check the sweetness, adding a touch more sugar if you’d like.
If you have ice, add it now, right before drinking, rather than earlier — adding it too soon dilutes the lassi while you’re still whisking.
Pour into a glass and drink cold.
recipes.money_hack: Making lassi with slightly thick, full-fat curd (if that’s what’s available) gives a richer result without needing to add anything extra.
recipes.swap_it: No cardamom? A few drops of rose water, if you have it, gives a different but pleasant flavour twist.
recipes.closing_line: Cold, sweet, and thick enough to almost count as lunch.

recipes.title: No-Cook Peanut Jaggery Bites
recipes.tagline: Small, chewy energy bites made from just peanuts and jaggery — no cooking required.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: These hold together purely from the warmth and pressure of your hands working the jaggery until it becomes slightly sticky — no heat, no syrup, just hand warmth doing all the work.
steps: Put the peanuts on a cutting board or in your palm. Crush them roughly using the flat side of a knife, the back of a spoon, or by pressing your palms together with the peanuts in between — you want a mix of small pieces and some finer crumb, not a completely uniform powder.
If your jaggery is in a hard block, grate it using a grater, or crush it into small bits with the back of a spoon — the finer this is, the more evenly it will bind with the peanuts later.
Put the crushed peanuts, jaggery, and a tiny pinch of salt into a bowl.

Mix with your hands for about 30 seconds — the warmth from your palms will start softening the jaggery slightly as you work it through the peanuts, and you’ll feel the mixture start to hold together a little.

Take a small portion of the mixture — about a tablespoon — and press it firmly between your palms, rolling it into a compact ball. Apply real pressure here; it’s that pressing and the warmth of your hands that binds everything together.
Repeat with the rest of the mixture, making 4 similar-sized bites.
Place the bites on a plate and let them sit for a few minutes to firm up slightly before eating.
recipes.money_hack: Make a slightly bigger batch and store in an airtight container — these keep for several days without needing refrigeration.
recipes.swap_it: Jaggery too hard to grate? Warm it very briefly (a few seconds) in the microwave to soften it before mixing.
recipes.cost_breakdown_text: Peanuts — ₹8, Jaggery — ₹6, Salt — negligible. Estimated total — ₹14.
recipes.closing_line: Two ingredients, genuinely no cooking, still tastes like you tried.

recipes.title: Butter Salt Rice
recipes.tagline: Rice, butter or ghee, and salt. That’s genuinely the whole recipe.
recipes.equipment_text: Microwave or one pan (to warm rice)
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Stirring the butter into the rice while it’s still properly hot — not just warm — is what melts it completely and coats every grain, instead of leaving unmelted lumps sitting on top.

ingredients.raw: Pinch of black pepper (optional, if you have it)
ingredients.name: black pepper

steps: Put the rice into a microwave-safe bowl, or into a pan if warming on the stove.

If using a microwave: heat on high for about 1 minute, then stir once, then heat for another 30 seconds if it’s not fully hot yet. If using a pan: put it on the stove on medium heat, add a small splash of water, and stir occasionally for about 2 minutes until steaming hot.
Check that the rice is properly hot all the way through, not just warm on the outside — if using a microwave, feel the middle of the bowl after stirring to make sure there are no cold spots.
While it’s still steaming hot, add the butter or ghee directly on top.
Stir immediately — the residual heat should melt it within a few seconds as you mix it through.
Add salt, tasting a small spoonful as you go, since salt is doing most of the flavour work here. Add pepper if using.
Give it one final stir to make sure everything is evenly mixed, then eat.
recipes.money_hack: Always keep a small block of butter or ghee in your room specifically for nights like this — it’s the single ingredient that turns ”just rice” into a real meal.
recipes.swap_it: No butter or ghee? A teaspoon of oil and a little extra salt still makes this edible and warm, if less rich.
recipes.closing_line: This still counts as dinner. No judgement here.

recipes.title: Sugar Roti
recipes.tagline: A roti with ghee and sugar — the emergency comfort food that tastes like being a kid again.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Making sure the roti is genuinely warm, not just at room temperature, lets the ghee melt in slightly rather than sitting as a cold, waxy layer on top.
steps: Put a dry pan on the stove and turn the flame to medium, or hold the roti directly over a low open flame using tongs.
Warm the roti for about 10 seconds on one side, then flip and warm the other side for 10 seconds too — you want it soft and slightly bendable, not stiff or cold.
Lay the warm roti flat on a plate.
Using a spoon, scoop the ghee and spread it evenly over one side while the roti is still warm — the warmth helps it melt in slightly rather than sitting as a solid layer.
Sprinkle the sugar evenly over the ghee, making sure it reaches right to the edges so every bite gets some sweetness.
Fold the roti in half, then in half again if you’d like it more compact, or roll it up from one side.
Eat immediately while it’s still warm — the sugar’s crunch and the ghee’s softness are both at their best right away.
recipes.money_hack: This recipe needs almost nothing, but if you have even one more ingredient — a banana, some peanuts — chopping it in makes it feel like an upgrade.
recipes.swap_it: No ghee? Butter works exactly the same way here.
recipes.closing_line: Someone probably made you this exact thing when you were small. It still works.

recipes.title: Jeera Water Rice
recipes.tagline: Plain rice, lifted by nothing more than a simple cumin tempering — the true last-resort meal.
recipes.why_youll_love_it: Letting the cumin seeds actually sizzle and turn a shade darker in the hot oil, rather than tossing them in with everything else at once, releases far more aroma than raw cumin ever could.
steps: Put your pan on the stove, add the oil, and turn the flame to medium.
Wait about 30 seconds until the oil looks hot — you can test this by flicking one drop of water into the pan; if it sizzles immediately, it’s ready.
Add the cumin seeds.
Wait for them to sizzle and turn a shade darker — this takes about 10–15 seconds, and it’s the entire flavour base of the dish, so don’t rush past it.
Add the cooked rice straight away, right after the cumin is ready.
Toss everything together well with your spoon, making sure the tempered oil coats every part of the rice rather than staying pooled at the bottom of the pan.
Add salt, tasting a small spoonful as you go.
Give it one final toss and eat — straight from the pan if that’s genuinely all the energy you have tonight.
recipes.money_hack: Keep a small jar of cumin seeds specifically as an emergency flavour booster — it costs very little and turns almost any plain starch into something with intention behind it.
recipes.swap_it: No cumin seeds? A pinch of any spice you have — even just black pepper — is better than nothing.
